knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(x,s\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), and set \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\). For \(r_p\in\mathbb R^m\), \(r_d,r_c\in\mathbb R^n\), and directions \(\Delta x,\Delta s\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta y\in\mathbb R^m\), consider
\[A\Delta x=r_p,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=r_d,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=r_c.\]
Eliminating \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta s\) gives
\[(AS^{-1}XA^{\mathsf T})\Delta y=r_p-AS^{-1}(r_c-Xr_d).\]
After solving for \(\Delta y\), recover
\[\Delta s=r_d-A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y,\qquad \Delta x=S^{-1}(r_c-X\Delta s).\]
The matrix \(AS^{-1}XA^{\mathsf T}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the explicitly dimensioned primal-dual Newton equations, eliminating primal and slack directions yields a symmetric positive-definite system for the dual direction when the constraint matrix has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Normal Equations

source_witnesses.locator: 8.6 Affine Scaling, Primal-Dual Path Following, and Predictor-Corrector Variants of Interior Point Methods p. 428

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and dual interior-point normal-equation reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic reductions of an LP interior-point KKT system and the sparsity tradeoff induced by dense columns or rows of the constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), with \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\), \(Y=\operatorname{Diag}(y)\), and \(W=\operatorname{Diag}(w)\) invertible. Eliminating \(\Delta x\) gives the \(m\)-dimensional primal normal equations
\[
-\bigl(Y^{-1}W+AXZ^{-1}A^T\bigr)\Delta y
=b-Ax-\mu Y^{-1}e-AXZ^{-1}\bigl(c-A^Ty+\mu X^{-1}e\bigr).
\]
Eliminating \(\Delta y\) instead gives the \(n\)-dimensional dual normal equations
\[
\bigl(A^TYW^{-1}A+X^{-1}Z\bigr)\Delta x
=c-A^Ty+\mu X^{-1}e+A^TYW^{-1}\bigl(b-Ax-\mu Y^{-1}e\bigr).
\]
For the primal Gram-type term,
\[
(AXZ^{-1}A^T)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^n a_{ik}\frac{x_k}{z_k}a_{jk}.
\]
Disjoint supports of rows \(i\) and \(j\) therefore force this entry to be zero, whereas overlapping supports permit a nonzero. Dense columns can destroy sparsity in the primal normal equations, while dense rows can destroy sparsity in the dual normal equations. Hence neither reduction is uniformly preferable; when both occur, direct factorization of the reduced KKT system may permit more favorable pivot ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the primal step gives an m-by-m primal normal-equation system, while eliminating the dual step gives an n-by-n dual normal-equation system. Entries of the primal Gram-type term are weighted inner products of rows of A, so disjoint row supports guarantee zeros. Dense columns can cause fill in the primal system, and dense rows can cause fill in the dual system. Thus neither form is always preferable; with both dense rows and dense columns, direct factorization of the reduced KKT system may offer better pivot ordering.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
X=\operatorname{Diag}(x),\ Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\text{ are invertible}
Y=\operatorname{Diag}(y),\ W=\operatorname{Diag}(w)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\text{ are invertible}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The KKT system has primal and dual normal-equation reductions, and their relative sparsity depends respectively on dense columns and dense rows of }A\text{.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(x,s\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), and set \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\). For \(r_p\in\mathbb R^m\), \(r_d,r_c\in\mathbb R^n\), and directions \(\Delta x,\Delta s\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Delta y\in\mathbb R^m\), eliminating \(\Delta s\) from
\[A\Delta x=r_p,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=r_d,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=r_c\]
yields
\[\begin{pmatrix}-X^{-1}S&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}r_d-X^{-1}r_c\\r_p\end{pmatrix}.\]
The eliminated direction is recovered by
\[\Delta s=X^{-1}(r_c-S\Delta x).\]
The coefficient matrix is symmetric and generally indefinite.

children.top_down_role: Reduced-coordinate linear systems built around null-space structure.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank and \(m<n\).
\(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(x_p\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(Ax_p=b\).
\(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) has full column rank and \(AZ=0\).
\(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric and \(g\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible vector has a unique representation \(x=x_p+Zp\), and stationarity of the quadratic model in null-space coordinates is the displayed reduced equation.

notation.meaning: Matrix whose columns form a basis of the null space of A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametrization of an affine constraint set by null-space coordinates.

source_refs.locator: 4-1. Systems of Equations with the Same Solution Set p. 69

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m<n\), let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), let \(x_p\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(Ax_p=b\), and let the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) form a basis of \(\ker A\). Then
\[\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}=\{x_p+Zp:p\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\}.\]
Let \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric and let \(g\in\mathbb R^n\). For the equality-constrained quadratic model
\[\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx+g^{\mathsf T}x,\]
substitution of \(x=x_p+Zp\) gives the reduced Hessian \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\), and stationarity in \(p\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\) is
\[(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)p=-Z^{\mathsf T}(Hx_p+g).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A null-space basis uniquely parametrizes every equality-feasible point; for an explicitly defined symmetric quadratic model, stationarity then reduces to a system in the null-space coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Representations

children.title: QR-Based Representations
children.top_down_role: Orthogonal-factorization representations used for rank-sensitive LP linear systems.

knowledge_statements.title: QR-Based Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal decomposition of equality constraints and their null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, with \(m\le n\), and take a complete QR factorization 
\[A^{\mathsf T}=Q\begin{pmatrix}R\\0\end{pmatrix}=Q_1R,\qquad Q=[Q_1\ Q_2],\]
where \(Q\) is orthogonal and \(R\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular. Then \(AQ_2=0\), so the columns of \(Q_2\) form an orthonormal basis of \(\ker A\). A particular solution of \(Ax=b\) is \(x_p=Q_1R^{-\mathsf T}b\), and every solution is 
\[x=Q_1R^{-\mathsf T}b+Q_2p.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete QR factorization supplies orthonormal range and null-space bases and directly parametrizes all solutions of the equality system.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank and \(m\le n\).
The QR factorization is complete, with \(R\) nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_2\) spans \(\ker A\), and the displayed formula represents every solution of \(Ax=b\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal bases for the range of the transpose and the null space

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\in\mathbb R^{k\times k}\) be nonsingular, \(E\in\mathbb R^{\ell\times k}\), \(D\in\mathbb R^{\ell\times\ell}\), \(f\in\mathbb R^k\), and \(g\in\mathbb R^\ell\). Consider the block system
\[\begin{pmatrix}H&E^{\mathsf T}\\E&-D\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}f\\g\end{pmatrix},\qquad (u,v)\in\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R^\ell.\]
Eliminating
\[u=H^{-1}(f-E^{\mathsf T}v)\]
produces
\[(D+EH^{-1}E^{\mathsf T})v=EH^{-1}f-g.\]
After solving the reduced equation, recover \(u\) from the elimination formula. The reduced representation is algebraically equivalent to the block system. Its practical suitability depends on the cost, sparsity, and numerical stability of applying \(H^{-1}\) and handling the Schur-complement coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For explicitly dimensioned blocks with a nonsingular eliminated block, block elimination gives an equivalent Schur-complement system followed by recovery of the eliminated variables.

children.title: Representation Selection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Rank, density, conditioning, plus dimension regimes governing representation choice.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Selection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning boundary between normal-equation and orthogonal representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank. In the spectral norm, 
\[\kappa_2(MM^{\mathsf T})=\kappa_2(M)^2.\]
Consequently, a normal-equation representation squares the singular-value condition number and may lose substantially more accuracy than an orthogonal QR representation when \(\kappa_2(M)\) is large. Normal equations remain attractive when their smaller positive-definite factorization preserves sparsity and the squared conditioning is acceptable. QR or an augmented formulation is favored when conditioning dominates cost; a null-space representation additionally requires a reliable basis whose construction and fill do not outweigh dimensional reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal equations trade a smaller positive-definite system for squared conditioning; QR, augmented, or null-space forms become preferable when accuracy or basis construction dominates.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) has full row rank.
Condition numbers use the matrix spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity \(\kappa_2(MM^{\mathsf T})=\kappa_2(M)^2\) marks a numerical boundary against normal-equation reduction.

notation.meaning: Spectral-norm condition number based on nonzero singular values

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the selection-boundary leaf, and the condition-number identity is correct for a full-row-rank rectangular matrix when the condition number uses its nonzero singular values. The broader recommendations comparing normal equations, QR, augmented systems, and null-space methods depend on sparsity, stability, and implementation tradeoffs and require a specific source.

children.title: Symbolic-Structure Reuse
children.top_down_role: Validity plus performance of reusing symbolic information across related factorizations.

Under these conditions the elimination tree, factor pattern, supernode partition, and workspace map are invariant, while factor entries are recomputed for each matrix.

Writing only positions in \(\mathcal F_s\) then loses required updates and cannot produce a valid factorization.

children.title: Minimum-Degree Orderings
children.top_down_role: Fill-reducing orderings based on evolving graph degree information.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite undirected graph representing a symmetric sparsity pattern.
Ties between minimum-degree vertices are resolved by a fixed rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output permutation is the exact minimum-degree elimination ordering for the specified tie rule.

notation.meaning: current filled graph after earlier eliminations
active degree of vertex v at step k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical exact minimum-degree ordering algorithm; exact authoritative locator unavailable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph-elimination version of minimum degree for symmetric sparse factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(G_1\) as the sparsity graph and \(\pi\) as empty. At step \(k\), choose an active vertex \(v_k\) minimizing \(d_k(v)\). Make the active neighbors of \(v_k\) a clique, delete \(v_k\), append \(v_k\) to \(\pi\), and update all affected exact degrees. Continue until no vertices remain and return \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact minimum degree repeatedly eliminates a current minimum-degree vertex, adds its fill clique, updates exact active degrees, and returns the elimination order.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-degree ordering for sparse Cholesky factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Cholesky fill-in, states the minimum-degree pivot heuristic and its local motivation, and records the hardness boundary for globally minimizing fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In sparse Cholesky factorization, fill-in occurs at a lower-triangular position $(i,j)$ when $M_{ij}=0$ but the corresponding entry of the Cholesky factor $L$ is nonzero. The minimum-degree heuristic repeatedly selects a diagonal pivot of minimum degree in the current remaining matrix, symmetrically moves its row and column to the next elimination position, and performs the elimination. Here the degree is the number of off-diagonal nonzeros in the pivot row or column. If the pivot has degree $d$, its outer-product update has a $d\times d$ nonzero structure, motivating the minimum-degree choice. Finding an ordering that globally minimizes fill-in is NP-complete in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fill-in consists of Cholesky-factor nonzeros at positions that were zero in the original matrix. Minimum-degree ordering repeatedly chooses a pivot having the fewest current off-diagonal nonzeros, symmetrically moves it to the next elimination position, and eliminates it. Its degree-d update has a d-by-d nonzero structure, which motivates the heuristic. Finding a globally minimum-fill ordering is NP-complete in general.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a symmetric sparse matrix undergoing Cholesky factorization.}
d\text{ is the number of off-diagonal nonzeros in the candidate pivot row or column of the current remaining matrix.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Minimum-degree ordering is the stated local fill-reduction heuristic, whereas computing a globally minimum-fill ordering is NP-complete in general.}

children.title: Approximate Minimum-Degree Orderings
children.top_down_role: Lower-cost approximations to minimum-degree ordering for large sparse systems.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite undirected sparsity graph.
The implementation maintains conservative or estimated degrees using quotient-graph equivalences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned permutation follows the chosen approximate-degree rule, but need not equal an exact minimum-degree ordering.

notation.meaning: active quotient graph at step k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic approximate minimum-degree formulation; implementation-specific degree estimator needs source

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the quotient representation \(Q_1\) of the sparsity graph. At step \(k\), select an active vertex or indistinguishable set minimizing the maintained estimate \(\widehat d_k\), eliminate it, update quotient elements and adjacency sets, absorb indistinguishable or dominated nodes when permitted, and recompute only affected degree estimates. Continue until all vertices are ordered, returning the concatenated permutation \(\pi\).

children.title: Nested-Dissection Orderings
children.top_down_role: Separator-based ordering choices for matrices with exploitable graph structure.

assumptions_latex: The sparsity graph admits recursively computed vertex separators.
Each separator disconnects its subgraph into components after removal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every component vertex precedes its separating vertices, yielding a valid nested-dissection permutation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical recursive separator ordering; exact authoritative locator unavailable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive separator ordering for symmetric sparse factorization graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a subgraph on \(V\), choose a separator \(S\subset V\) such that removing \(S\) produces components with vertex sets \(V_1,ldots,V_t\). Recursively order each induced subgraph on \(V_i\), concatenate those component orderings in a fixed order, and append the vertices of \(S\). For a base-size subgraph, use a fixed local ordering. The top-level concatenation is \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested dissection recursively orders disconnected components first and their separating vertices last, using a fixed local ordering at small subproblems.

children.title: Ordering Selection Regimes

children.title: Dense-Row Handling
children.top_down_role: Isolation, delayed treatment, or special storage for unusually dense rows.

assumptions_latex: A small set of rows has substantially larger structural degree than typical rows.
The remaining sparse core can be factored with a sparse direct method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sparse core is factored without immediately expanding dense-row interactions, and the deferred rows are recovered through a smaller correction system.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic deferred dense-row and Schur-complement strategy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deferred treatment of a small dense-row block in sparse linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After a row permutation, write the system as \(\begin{pmatrix}A_s\\R\end{pmatrix}x=\begin{pmatrix}b_s\\b_R\end{pmatrix}\), where \(R\) has \(r\) dense rows. Factor the sparse core contribution first, retaining the action needed to form the dense-row Schur or bordered correction. Solve the resulting correction system of dimension proportional to \(r\), then recover \(x\) by sparse triangular solves and correction updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate a few dense rows, factor the sparse core, solve a small bordered or Schur-complement correction, and recover the full solution without premature fill expansion.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Row Handling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Dense-Row Handling, but the vertically partitioned system may be rectangular and does not by itself define a factorizable sparse-core operator or a Schur complement. children.title: Dense-Column Handling
children.top_down_role: Isolation, partitioning, or special treatment for unusually dense columns.

assumptions_latex: A small set of columns has substantially larger structural degree than typical columns.
The complementary columns define a factorable sparse core.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense-column effects are confined to a low-dimensional update or border while sparse-core factorization retains its sparsity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic bordering and low-rank dense-column strategy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bordered or low-rank treatment of a small dense-column block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Permute columns so that \(A=[A_s\;D]\), where \(D\) contains \(d\) dense columns. Analyze and factor the sparse-core operator induced by \(A_s\), and represent the contribution of \(D\) as a border or rank-at-most-\(d\) update. Form and solve the corresponding dense correction system, apply sparse triangular solves for the core variables, and assemble the solution in the original column order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move a few dense columns to a border or low-rank update, factor the sparse core, solve a small correction, and restore the original variable order.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Column Handling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Dense-Column Handling, but merely partitioning \(A=[A_s\;D]\) does not uniquely define a sparse-core operator, a rank-at-most-\(d\) update to the factorized system, or a correction system. children.title: Dense-Structure Crossover Regimes
children.top_down_role: Density thresholds plus cost tradeoffs governing sparse versus dense treatment.

assumptions_latex: Both sparse and dense kernels are available for the same frontal or trailing block.
Their time and memory costs can be estimated consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A block should cross to dense treatment exactly when it is feasible and its estimated total cost is smaller than continued sparse processing.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic cost-and-memory crossover condition; thresholds are hardware dependent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational crossover criterion; concrete thresholds depend on hardware and sparse-kernel implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a remaining block or front, estimate \(C_s\), the cost of continued sparse processing, and \(C_d=C_{\mathrm{convert}}+C_{\mathrm{dense}}\), the cost of packing and applying dense kernels. Cross to dense treatment when \(C_d<C_s\), the dense workspace fits within \(M\), and the conversion does not violate the factorization's pivoting constraints. Otherwise retain sparse storage and kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switch a block to dense kernels when conversion plus dense work is cheaper than sparse work, memory is sufficient, and pivoting constraints remain valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Structure Crossover Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the Dense-Structure Crossover Regimes leaf, but the claim that crossover occurs exactly when the estimated dense cost is smaller is only valid relative to a calibrated and sufficiently complete cost model. children.title: Sparse Pivot Selection
children.top_down_role: Pivot choices balancing sparsity, numerical magnitude, plus structural constraints.

assumptions_latex: At each elimination step a nonempty set of structurally admissible pivot candidates is available.
Candidate magnitudes and predicted fill costs can be evaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted pivot satisfies the stated stability threshold and minimizes the declared sparsity cost among candidates passing that threshold.

notation.meaning: predicted fill cost of candidate pair (i,j)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thresholded sparse pivot selection balancing numerical magnitude and predicted fill.

source_refs.locator: 1. Solving Systems of Equations: LU-Factorization p. 124

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At step \(k\), form the structurally admissible candidate set \(C_k\). Retain candidates \((i,j)\in C_k\) satisfying \(|(A_k)_{ij}|\geq\tau\max_{r}|(A_k)_{rj}|\). Among retained candidates choose one minimizing \(\phi_k(i,j)\), interchange it into pivot position, and perform the elimination update. If none passes, delay the column, relax the policy under explicit limits, or report pivot rejection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse pivot selection filters structurally admissible candidates by a numerical threshold, then chooses a passing pivot with low predicted fill or reports a controlled rejection.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Pivot Selection

source_witnesses.locator: 1. Solving Systems of Equations: LU-Factorization p. 124

children.title: Factorization Stability Control
children.top_down_role: Thresholds, monitoring signals, plus safeguards used to maintain reliable factors.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and is factorized in floating-point arithmetic as \(PAQ=LU\).
Residual, growth, and pivot thresholds \(\tau_r,\tau_g,\tau_p>0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{stable}(L,U)\iff \rho\le\tau_r\land g\le\tau_g\land p_{\min}\ge\tau_p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A diagnostic acceptance predicate for a computed sparse factorization, not a universal choice of thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a computed sparse factorization \(PAQ=LU\), define the scaled residual \(\rho=\lVert PAQ-LU\rVert/(\lVert A\rVert+\lVert L\rVert\lVert U\rVert)\), the element-growth factor \(g=\lVert U\rVert_{\max}/\lVert A\rVert_{\max}\), and the minimum scaled accepted pivot \(p_{\min}\). The factorization passes stability control exactly when \(\rho\le\tau_r\), \(g\le\tau_g\), and \(p_{\min}\ge\tau_p\). Failure of any test requires rejection, a more stable pivoting regime, or refactorization; the numerical thresholds are implementation parameters tied to precision and requested solve accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a computed factorization only when its scaled residual and element growth are small enough and every accepted pivot is sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Stability Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited chapter locator is inspectable only as a table-of-contents entry and does not support this exact three-test acceptance predicate. In addition, the scaling used to define the minimum scaled pivot is unspecified, so the stated condition is not mathematically reproducible. A numerical linear algebra source or solver specification supporting the residual, growth, and scaled-pivot tests is required.

children.title: Pivot-Rejection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Numerical or structural conditions causing candidate pivots to be rejected.

assumptions_latex: At elimination step \(k\), \(A^{(k)}=(a_{ij}^{(k)})\) is the current elimination matrix and \(S_k\) is the set of candidate row indices permitted by the structural and ordering rules.
A relative threshold \(u\in(0,1]\) and an absolute floor \(p_0>0\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(S_k\ne\varnothing\), then \(a_{ik}^{(k)}\) is admissible exactly when \(i\in S_k\) and \(|a_{ik}^{(k)}|\ge\max\{p_0,u m_k\}\), where \(m_k=\max_{j\in S_k}|a_{jk}^{(k)}|\); if \(S_k=\varnothing\), the current pivoting regime fails structurally.

notation.meaning: current elimination matrix at step k
largest candidate magnitude when the candidate set is nonempty

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold rejection within a structurally admissible sparse-pivot set; an empty structural candidate set is distinguished from numerical rejection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At elimination step \(k\), let \(A^{(k)}=(a_{ij}^{(k)})\) be the current elimination matrix and let \(S_k\) contain the candidate row indices permitted by the structural and sparse-ordering rules. If \(S_k\ne\varnothing\), put \(m_k=\max_{j\in S_k}|a_{jk}^{(k)}|\). A candidate \(a_{ik}^{(k)}\) is numerically admissible exactly when \(i\in S_k\) and \(|a_{ik}^{(k)}|\ge\max\{p_0,u m_k\}\), where \(u\in(0,1]\) is the relative threshold and \(p_0>0\) is the absolute floor. Candidates outside \(S_k\), below the relative threshold, or below the absolute floor are rejected. If \(S_k=\varnothing\), or if no member of a nonempty \(S_k\) satisfies the numerical test, the current pivoting regime fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reject candidates excluded by the structural rules or lying below the relative or absolute numerical threshold; the pivoting regime fails if no admissible candidate remains.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivot-Rejection Regimes

children.title: Unstable-Factor Recovery
children.top_down_role: Refactorization, reordering, rescaling, or method responses after factor instability.

assumptions_latex: A factorization has failed at least one stability test.
The original matrix and a stronger permissible pivoting or scaling configuration remain available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is either a newly accepted factorization or an explicit numerical-singularity report.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery by fresh factorization under progressively stronger numerical safeguards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rejected factorization of \(A\), choose an ordered list \(\mathcal{C}=(c_1,\ldots,c_s)\) of recovery configurations, such as equilibration, tighter pivot thresholds, expanded pivot searches, and fresh symbolic ordering. For \(j=1,\ldots,s\), discard the unstable numerical factors, refactorize the original matrix under \(c_j\), and evaluate \(\operatorname{stable}(L_j,U_j)\). Stop at the first accepted pair and return \((L_j,U_j,c_j)\). If no configuration produces acceptable factors, report numerical singularity or instability rather than continuing solves with the rejected factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard unstable factors and refactorize under progressively stronger scaling, pivoting, or ordering safeguards; otherwise report numerical singularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Unstable-Factor Recovery

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited chapter locator does not substantiate the proposed ordered recovery configurations or the claim that exhausting them warrants a numerical-singularity report. Failure of a finite solver-configured recovery list need not establish numerical singularity. A solver or numerical factorization source specifying the recovery protocol and terminal status is required.
