notation.meaning: feasible set of row constraint i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conflict attribution by the types of members in an irreducible infeasible subsystem
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attributes an irreducible conflict entirely to explicit model rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let model restrictions be partitioned into row-feasible sets \(H_i\) and variable-bound literals \(L_j\). A constraint conflict attribution is an irreducible infeasible subsystem containing only row constraints: there is a nonempty set \(I\) such that \(\bigcap_{i\in I}H_i=\varnothing\), while \(\bigcap_{i\in I\setminus\{k\}}H_i\neq\varnothing\) for every \(k\in I\). No bound literal is a member of the attributed subsystem, even if bounds occur elsewhere in the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint conflict is a minimal infeasible subsystem composed solely of explicit row constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Conflict Attribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently classifies a row-only IIS and fits the terminal container, but the row-versus-bound attribution taxonomy lacks a targeted source.

children.title: Bound Conflict Attribution
children.top_down_role: Attribution of infeasibility evidence to variable bounds.

assumptions_latex: Model restrictions are partitioned into row constraints \(H_i\) and bound literals \(L_j\).
The selected conflict is required to be inclusion-minimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound conflict has the form \((\varnothing,J)\), with \(\bigcap_{j\in J}L_j=\varnothing\) and every proper selected subfamily feasible.

notation.meaning: feasible set of bound literal j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conflict attribution by the types of members in an irreducible infeasible subsystem
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers contradictions formed entirely by lower or upper bound literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each lower or upper variable bound be represented by a feasible-set literal \(L_j\). A bound conflict attribution is an irreducible infeasible subsystem containing only such literals: for some nonempty \(J\), \(\bigcap_{j\in J}L_j=\varnothing\), whereas \(\bigcap_{j\in J\setminus\{k\}}L_j\neq\varnothing\) for every \(k\in J\). In the usual single lower and upper bound representation, \(x_q\geq \ell_q\) and \(x_q\leq u_q\) form a bound-only conflict when \(\ell_q>u_q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound conflict is a minimal infeasible subsystem made only of lower or upper bound literals.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound Conflict Attribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound-only IIS definition and example are mathematically coherent and locally appropriate, but no source supports this attribution convention.

children.title: Mixed Conflict Attribution
children.top_down_role: Attribution for conflicts involving interacting constraints and bounds.

assumptions_latex: Model restrictions are partitioned into row constraints \(H_i\) and bound literals \(L_j\).
The selected conflict is required to be inclusion-minimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A mixed conflict has \(I\neq\varnothing\), \(J\neq\varnothing\), and \(\bigcap_{i\in I}H_i\cap\bigcap_{j\in J}L_j=\varnothing\), minimally.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conflict attribution by the types of members in an irreducible infeasible subsystem
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attributes infeasibility jointly to model rows and variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed conflict attribution is an irreducible infeasible subsystem containing at least one row constraint and at least one bound literal. Thus nonempty sets \(I\) and \(J\) satisfy \(\bigcap_{i\in I}H_i\cap\bigcap_{j\in J}L_j=\varnothing\), but removing any one selected \(H_i\) or \(L_j\) makes the remaining intersection nonempty. Neither the selected rows alone nor the selected bounds alone need be infeasible; the contradiction arises from their joint restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed conflict is a minimal infeasible subsystem containing both row constraints and variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Conflict Attribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixed row-and-bound IIS definition fits the leaf and states inclusion-minimality adequately, but it has no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Elastic Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Repair interfaces based on explicit elasticity for selected model restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Elastic Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted one-sided elastic formulation for inequality rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given inequalities \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\), introduce \(s_i\geq0\) for each relaxable row and solve \[\min_{x,s}\;c^{\mathsf T}x+\rho\sum_i w_i s_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i+s_i,\quad s_i\geq0.\] Protected rows are imposed without relaxation. If the resulting LP is solved to certified optimality, output an optimizer \((x^\rho,s^\rho)\); each positive \(s_i^\rho\) identifies and quantifies the additive relaxation assigned to row \(i\). An equality requires separate nonnegative positive and negative elastic variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elastic relaxation adds penalized nonnegative violation variables to relaxable rows. When the resulting LP has a certified optimum, its elastic variables report the selected row relaxations.
assumptions_latex: The LP has inequalities \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\), objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), weights \(w_i>0\), and penalty \(\rho>0\).
The elastic LP is feasible, has a finite attained optimum, and is solved to certified optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns an optimizer \((x^\rho,s^\rho)\), and each \(s_i^\rho\) reports the additive relaxation assigned to row \(i\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative elastic variable for relaxable row i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weighted elastic-variable LP construction

children.title: Feasibility Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Broader model modifications intended to recover a feasible formulation.

assumptions_latex: The relaxable system is \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\) with weights \(w_i>0\).
At least one point satisfies all protected, nonrelaxable restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \((x^F,s^F)\) minimizes weighted total violation, and the original system is feasible exactly when \(\sum_i w_i s_i^F=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard phase-I weighted feasibility-relaxation formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-I repair minimizes violation independently of the original objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Construct the phase-I LP \[\min_{x,s}\;\sum_i w_i s_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i\leq s_i,
\quad s_i\geq0,\] together with every protected restriction. Solve it to certified optimality and return \((x^F,s^F)\). The vector \(s^F\) is a minimum-weight additive repair for the chosen representation. If its objective is zero, \(x^F\) is feasible for every original row; if it is positive, the original system is infeasible under the protected restrictions and the positive components describe one optimal relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility relaxation minimizes weighted violations; zero optimum proves feasibility, while positive slacks describe an optimal additive repair.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The phase-I algorithm and its zero-optimum feasibility equivalence are appropriate under the stated protected-set assumption, but no cited source supports the formulation or interpretation.

children.title: Relaxation Penalty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Penalty structures governing the relative acceptability of model violations.

assumptions_latex: Violation variables satisfy \(s\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and weights satisfy \(w_i>0\).
The feasible repair set \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected regime determines the repair set \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,s)\in\mathcal R}\Phi(s)\), and different regimes can select different repairs.

notation.meaning: feasible set of repaired points and violations

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard norm and lexicographic penalty regimes for feasibility repair
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares aggregate, worst-case, and priority-ordered repair penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Common relaxation penalties are the weighted aggregate penalty \(\Phi_1(s)=\sum_i w_i s_i\), the worst-case penalty \(\Phi_\infty(s)=\max_i w_i s_i\), and a lexicographic penalty. For priority blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_q\), the lexicographic regime sequentially minimizes \(\sum_{i\in B_k}w_i s_i\) over the minimizers retained from levels \(1,
\ldots,k-1\). A finite scalar penalty \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\rho\Phi(s)\) trades repair against the original objective, whereas phase-I minimization of \(\Phi(s)\) gives repair precedence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty regimes minimize total violation, worst violation, or ordered priority blocks; finite penalties may trade feasibility repair against the original objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Penalty Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate kind for this catalogue of penalty regimes, and the formulas are coherent, but the aggregate, worst-case, lexicographic, and finite-penalty distinctions lack a supporting citation.

children.title: Repair Interpretability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where a relaxed solution provides limited guidance for model repair.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair Interpretability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal repairs quantify a chosen penalty model, not necessarily causal responsibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the infeasible restrictions \(x\leq0\) and \(x\geq2\), the equal-weight one-sided total violation is \((x)_++(2-x)_+=2\) for every \(x\in[0,2]\). Minimum-violation repairs may therefore assign relaxation to the first restriction, the second restriction, or both. Raw slack penalties can also change when a row is multiplied by a positive scalar unless its weight is transformed correspondingly. An optimal relaxation vector is interpretable only relative to the selected scaling, weights, protected set, penalty regime, and tie-breaking rule; it need not identify a unique or representation-invariant cause of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-violation repairs can be nonunique and scaling-dependent, so their positive slacks do not by themselves identify a unique causal responsibility.
assumptions_latex: Repairs are selected by minimizing a weighted one-sided violation objective.
Causal attribution is expected to be invariant under equivalent row scaling and optimizer choice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal relaxation vector need not identify a unique or representation-invariant cause of infeasibility.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-constraint counterexample demonstrates nonuniqueness of minimum-violation attribution

children.title: Borderline Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Solutions whose feasibility classification is sensitive to tolerance or validation context.

assumptions_latex: A normalized primal violation measure \(\eta_p(x)\geq0\) is fixed.
Declared thresholds satisfy \(0\leq\tau_{\mathrm{acc}}<\tau_{\mathrm{rej}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Borderline feasibility is the condition \(\tau_{\mathrm{acc}}<\eta_p(x)\leq\tau_{\mathrm{rej}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a tolerance band rather than exact mathematical feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inequalities \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\), let \(\eta_p(x)\) be a declared scale-normalized maximum violation, such as \(\max_i (a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i)_+/(1+|b_i|)\). The point is accepted as feasible when \(\eta_p(x)\leq\tau_{\mathrm{acc}}\), rejected under the selected policy when \(\eta_p(x)>\tau_{\mathrm{rej}}\), and classified as borderline feasible when \(\tau_{\mathrm{acc}}<\eta_p(x)\leq\tau_{\mathrm{rej}}\). This classification depends on scaling and declared tolerances and is not exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is borderline feasible when its normalized violation lies between declared acceptance and rejection thresholds.
knowledge_statements.title: Borderline Feasibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and tolerance-band formulation fit the leaf, but the cited general implementation chapter does not specifically support the two-threshold classification or the proposed normalization. These are solver-policy conventions requiring a targeted source.

children.title: Near Optimality
children.top_down_role: Solutions close to requested optimality without supporting an unqualified optimal claim.

assumptions_latex: The primal LP is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\).
The dual variables satisfy the representation \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\) approximately, with \(s\geq0\).
Declared tolerances \(\tau_p,\tau_d,\tau_g\geq0\) and normalization conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The triple is near optimal when \(\eta_p\leq\tau_p\), \(\eta_d\leq\tau_d\), and \(\eta_g\leq\tau_g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-and-gap certificate for standard-form primal-dual LP candidates.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate \((x,y,s)\) with \(x\geq0\) and \(s\geq0\), compute normalized diagnostics from \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\), and \(g=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y\). Let \(\eta_p\), \(\eta_d\), and \(\eta_g\) be their declared normalized magnitudes. The candidate supplies a near-optimality certificate when \(\eta_p\leq\tau_p\), \(\eta_d\leq\tau_d\), and \(\eta_g\leq\tau_g\). Exact zero residuals and zero gap recover the standard primal-dual optimality certificate; positive tolerances certify only the stated numerical acceptance regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near optimality requires small normalized primal residual, dual residual, and primal-dual gap under explicitly declared tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Near Optimality

source_witnesses.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

children.title: Feasibility–Optimality Classification
children.top_down_role: Interactions between marginal feasibility and near-optimal objective quality.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Residual norms and tolerances are evaluated in one declared scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\wedge D\wedge G\Longrightarrow\text{accepted optimality at the declared tolerances}.\)

notation.meaning: Declared primal-feasibility, dual-feasibility, and optimality-gap tolerances.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based classification of a primal-dual LP candidate; failed tests do not certify infeasibility.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), and let \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n	imes\mathbb R^m	imes\mathbb R^n\) be a candidate. Given \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g\ge0\), define \(P\) by \(\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_p\) and \(x\ge-\varepsilon_p\mathbf1\); define \(D\) by \(\|A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\|\le\varepsilon_d\) and \(s\ge-\varepsilon_d\mathbf1\); and define \(G\) by \(|c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y|\le\varepsilon_g(1+|c^{\mathsf T}x|+|b^{\mathsf T}y|)\). Classify the candidate as accepted optimal when \(P\wedge D\wedge G\) holds, primal-feasible only when \(P\wedge
eg D\) holds, dual-feasible only when \(
eg P\wedge D\) holds, primal-dual feasible but optimality-uncertified when \(P\wedge D\wedge
eg G\) holds, and otherwise uncertified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declared primal residual, dual residual, sign, and duality-gap tests classify a candidate as accepted optimal, one-sided feasible, primal-dual feasible without an optimality certificate, or uncertified.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility–Optimality Classification

source_witnesses.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled–Unscaled Status Disagreement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status disagreement caused by applying noninvariant residual thresholds before and after diagonal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_r\) and \(D_c\) be nonsingular diagonal matrices and set \(\widetilde A=D_rAD_c\), \(\widetilde b=D_rb\), and \(x=D_c\widetilde x\). The scaled primal residual is \(\widetilde r_p=D_r(Ax-b)\), whereas the unscaled residual is \(r_p=Ax-b\). Thus an absolute test may satisfy \(\|\widetilde r_p\|\le\widetilde\varepsilon_p\) while \(\|r_p\|>\varepsilon_p\), or conversely. Such a candidate has scaled–unscaled status disagreement and must not receive an unqualified feasibility or optimality status until the original-model tests are evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal scaling can make a candidate pass scaled residual tests but fail original-model tests; final acceptance therefore requires an explicit unscaled check.
assumptions_latex: \(D_r\) and \(D_c\) are nonsingular diagonal scaling matrices.
Scaled and unscaled residual tests use declared norms and thresholds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf1_{\{\|\widetilde r_p\|\le\widetilde\varepsilon_p\}}\ne\mathbf1_{\{\|r_p\|\le\varepsilon_p\}}\Longrightarrow\text{status disagreement}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual transformation is mathematically consistent with the stated variable scaling, and failure_boundary fits the container. An authoritative solver-scaling source is still required for the status-disagreement interpretation and the requirement that original-model testing precede an unqualified status.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-but-Postsolve-Infeasible Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-model optimality does not survive acceptance when postsolve reconstruction violates the original LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a presolved LP have reduced variable \(z\) and reconstruction map \(x=P(z)\) into the original model \(Ax=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\). Even if \(z\) satisfies every reduced primal, dual, and gap tolerance, the reconstructed point is postsolve infeasible whenever \(\|AP(z)-b\|>\varepsilon_p\) or \(P(z)\notin[\ell-\varepsilon_p\mathbf1,u+\varepsilon_p\mathbf1]\). In that event, “optimal” is valid only for the reduced numerical model; it is not an accepted optimal solution of the original LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced optimum is rejected for the original LP if reconstruction violates an original constraint or bound beyond tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is the implemented postsolve reconstruction map.
Original-model feasibility is tested after all presolve transformations are reversed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(z)\notin\mathcal F_{\varepsilon_p}\Longrightarrow P(z)\text{ is not an accepted original-model optimum}.\)

notation.meaning: Original feasible set enlarged by the declared tolerance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately describes a failure boundary, but the implemented reconstruction map, tolerance enlargement, and distinction between reduced-model and original-model status require a specific presolve/postsolve source.

children.title: False-Precision Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Reported accuracy that exceeds the credible information supported by the computation.

knowledge_statements.title: False-Precision Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reported digits beyond the attainable backward-error floor lack certificate value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) be unit roundoff and let \(\eta>0\) be a justified lower estimate of the normalized residual floor produced by conditioning, data representation, and finite-precision kernels. If a solver reports accuracy \(\varepsilon<\eta\) solely because iterates or objective values cease changing, while the independently recomputed certificate residual \(\rho\) satisfies \(\rho>\varepsilon\), then the extra reported digits constitute false precision. The result may still be acceptable at tolerance \(\rho\), but it is not certified at \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stagnant iterates or objective values do not justify digits beyond the independently measured residual and attainable numerical floor.
assumptions_latex: All residuals are normalized in a fixed, documented manner.
\(\eta\) accounts for finite precision and estimated conditioning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon<\eta\le\rho\Longrightarrow\text{no certificate at tolerance }\varepsilon.\)

notation.meaning: Unit roundoff of the working arithmetic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits, but no source establishes the proposed residual-floor model. Moreover, the premise states only that both the requested tolerance and measured residual straddle the tolerance, whereas the conclusion additionally assumes the unestablished ordering \(\eta\le\rho\). A numerical-error-analysis source and a corrected ordering hypothesis are required.

children.title: Over-Tight Tolerance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Accuracy settings that demand more than the model or numerical environment can reliably support.

knowledge_statements.title: Over-Tight Tolerance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A requested tolerance is over-tight when it lies below a justified numerical error floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed LP instance, arithmetic, scaling, and solver implementation, let \(\eta_{\mathrm{floor}}>0\) denote a validated lower bound or conservative estimate for the attainable normalized certificate residual. A requested stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon_{m req}\) is in the over-tight regime when \(0<\varepsilon_{m req}<\eta_{\mathrm{floor}}\). In this regime, failure to meet the requested tolerance is not by itself evidence that the exact LP is infeasible or lacks an optimum; it indicates that the requested numerical certificate exceeds the demonstrated resolution of the computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tolerance below the estimated attainable residual floor demands more accuracy than the chosen numerical computation can justify.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta_{\mathrm{floor}}\) is estimated using the declared arithmetic, scaling, and residual normalization.
The exact LP status is logically distinct from numerical stopping status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\varepsilon_{\rm req}<\eta_{\mathrm{floor}}\Longrightarrow\varepsilon_{\rm req}\text{ is over-tight}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind matches the terminal container, but the central quantity is an implementation-dependent attainable residual floor. A source must define or justify how such a positive bound or conservative estimate is obtained for the declared arithmetic, scaling, and residual normalization.

children.title: Tolerance-Induced Solver Failure
children.top_down_role: Performance or status failures attributable primarily to excessive accuracy demands.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Induced Solver Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An unattainable success threshold can produce numerical failure despite existence of an exact solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose solver success requires a normalized certificate residual \(\rho_k\le\varepsilon_{m req}\), but finite-precision iterates satisfy \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\rho_k\ge\eta_{\mathrm{floor}}>0\). If \(\varepsilon_{m req}<\eta_{\mathrm{floor}}\), the success test cannot eventually hold, even when the exact LP has an optimal primal–dual solution. Termination by iteration limit, stagnation, or numerical-error status is therefore tolerance-induced unless an independent certificate establishes genuine infeasibility, unboundedness, or another mathematical failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the requested tolerance lies below the residual floor, a solver can fail numerically even though the exact LP is solvable.
assumptions_latex: Success is conditioned on the displayed residual threshold.
The residual sequence has the stated positive finite-precision floor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon_{\rm req}<\eta_{\mathrm{floor}}\Longrightarrow\rho_k\le\varepsilon_{\rm req}\text{ cannot hold eventually}.\)

notation.meaning: Normalized certificate residual at iteration k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymptotic residual premise supports failure of the requested success test, but it does not establish that any iteration-limit, stagnation, or numerical-error termination was caused solely by the tolerance. A solver-termination source and narrower causal formulation are required. The failure_boundary kind otherwise fits.

children.title: LP Solver Method Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection among primal simplex, dual simplex, interior-point, first-order, and structure-specialized engines using required artifacts, model regime, solve sequence, accuracy, and resource constraints.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Families of LP algorithms; Choice of solvers and algorithms
LP solver choices and crossover controls

children.title: Basic-Solution Requirements
children.top_down_role: Method-selection requirements for returning a usable basis-associated solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic-Solution Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Artifact requirements for a basic feasible solution in equality standard form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), a basic feasible solution artifact consists of an index set \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\), together with \(x_N=0\) and \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\), where \(N=B^c\). Numerically, the artifact must also declare feasibility and nonsingularity tolerances; returning only an interior feasible point does not meet the basic-solution requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic-solution artifact must identify a nonsingular basis and the associated feasible basic and zero nonbasic variables.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The LP is represented in equality standard form.

notation.meaning: Basic and complementary nonbasic index sets.
Submatrix formed by the basic columns.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard-form basic feasible solution requirements are mathematically precise and condition is an appropriate content kind, but the record supplies no textbook definition or theorem locator as required by the evidence contract.

children.title: Vertex-Solution Requirements
children.top_down_role: Method-selection requirements for returning a vertex solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Solution Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric artifact requirements for a vertex of a standard-form feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). A feasible point \(x\in P\) is a vertex precisely when the only vector \(d\in\ker A\) satisfying \(d_i=0\) for every active nonnegativity constraint \(i\) with \(x_i=0\) is \(d=0\). Equivalently, \(x\) cannot be expressed as \(x=\lambda x^1+(1-\lambda)x^2\) for distinct \(x^1,x^2\in P\) and \(0<\lambda<1\). A vertex artifact must provide \(x\) and enough active-constraint information to verify this rank condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is feasible and admits no nonzero two-sided feasible displacement; active constraints must isolate the point.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedron in equality standard form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\iff\{d:Ad=0,\ d_i=0\text{ whenever }x_i=0\}=\{0\}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided feasible-displacement characterization is correct for the displayed standard-form polyhedron, and condition fits the artifact-requirement container. A specific polyhedral vertex characterization source is required.

children.title: Basis–Vertex Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model or solver regimes where basis artifacts and vertex requirements do not align cleanly.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis–Vertex Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form equivalence, with degeneracy and representation dependence made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) be nonempty and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). Then \(x\in P\) is a vertex of \(P\) if and only if \(x\) is a basic feasible solution for some nonsingular \(m\)-column submatrix of \(A\). The correspondence is not one-to-one: a degenerate vertex may be represented by multiple bases. Outside equality standard form, “basis” depends on the chosen slack-variable and active-constraint representation, and a polyhedron containing a line may have no vertices at all.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank standard-form polyhedron, vertices equal basic feasible solutions, but degenerate vertices can have multiple bases and representation matters.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ne\varnothing\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
Basic solutions are defined using the displayed equality-standard-form representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\iff x\text{ is a basic feasible solution}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The full-row-rank standard-form basis-vertex equivalence and degeneracy qualification are standard, and theorem is the correct content kind. No source locator is supplied for either the equivalence or its representation-dependent boundary statements.

children.title: Dual-Solution Requirements
children.top_down_role: Method-selection requirements for usable dual solution information.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Required primal–dual data for certifying an LP optimum and supporting postoptimality analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), a dual-solution artifact supplies \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(s\in\mathbb R^n\). It certifies exact optimality together with \(x\) when primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=0\) hold. A numerical artifact must instead report the primal residual, dual residual, sign violations, and normalized duality gap under declared tolerances; dual multipliers without these checks are not a complete certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A usable dual artifact includes multipliers, slacks, and residual and gap checks sufficient to verify primal–dual optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Primal and dual use the displayed sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0,\ c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\Longrightarrow x,y,s\text{ are optimal}.\)

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

children.title: Ranging Requirements
children.top_down_role: Method-selection requirements for allowable coefficient or right-hand-side ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Ranging Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-basis allowable ranges for simultaneous right-hand-side or objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be an optimal basis for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with \(x_B=B^{-1}b\ge0\) and \(r_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\ge0\). For \(b(\delta)=b+\delta d\), the same basis remains primal feasible exactly while \(B^{-1}(b+\delta d)\ge0\). For \(c(\delta)=c+\delta q\), it remains dual feasible exactly while \(c_N+\delta q_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}(c_B+\delta q_B)\ge0\). A ranging artifact must report the maximal interval of \(\delta\) satisfying the relevant inequalities and identify the fixed basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ranging reports the maximal perturbation interval on which a specified optimal basis preserves primal or dual feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular and primal–dual optimal at \(\delta=0\).
Only the stated one-parameter perturbation is applied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I=\{\delta:\text{the displayed fixed-basis feasibility inequalities hold}\}\text{ is the allowable range}.\)

notation.meaning: Matrix of columns in the fixed optimal basis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-basis right-hand-side and objective perturbation inequalities are internally consistent, and representation fits a ranging artifact. A specific authoritative sensitivity-ranging section or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Sensitivity Requirements
children.top_down_role: Method-selection requirements for local response or perturbation information.

knowledge_statements.title: Sensitivity Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local value derivatives require primal–dual solutions and stability of the active optimal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(b,c)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Suppose an optimal basis \(B\) remains primal and dual feasible for all sufficiently small perturbations under consideration, with \(x_B=B^{-1}b\), \(x_N=0\), and \(y=B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\). Then for right-hand-side direction \(d\) and objective direction \(q\), \(v(b+td,c)=v(b,c)+t y^{\mathsf T}d\) and \(v(b,c+tq)=v(b,c)+t x^{\mathsf T}q\) locally. Without basis stability or uniqueness, a single derivative may fail to exist and the relevant optimal solution set must be reported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable optimal primal and dual solutions give local value sensitivities; degeneracy or changing bases can make sensitivity set-valued.
assumptions_latex: The LP has an optimal basis that stays optimal for sufficiently small stated perturbations.
Perturbed problems remain feasible and bounded locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_bv[d]=y^{\mathsf T}d\quad\text{and}\quad D_cv[q]=x^{\mathsf T}q\text{ under local basis stability}.\)

notation.meaning: Optimal value as a function of right-hand side and objective.
Locally stable primal and dual optimal solutions.

source_refs.locator: 4.4. Optimal dual variables as marginal costs p. 155

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4. Optimal dual variables as marginal costs p. 155

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited marginal-cost section specifically supports right-hand-side sensitivity but does not supply the required locator for objective-coefficient sensitivity. The notation \(D_bv\) and \(D_cv\) also needs clarification as a local two-sided derivative under basis stability or as a directional derivative. Because source coverage affects the combined mathematical claim, an additional authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Postoptimality Artifact Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of solver outputs with requested ranging or sensitivity workflows.

knowledge_statements.title: Postoptimality Artifact Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for basis-dependent LP sensitivity and ranging artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), an artifact supports basis-dependent postoptimality analysis when it supplies an index set \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of cardinality \(m\), with \(A_B\) nonsingular, such that \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\), \(x_N=0\), \(y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), and \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\), where \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\). These identities give \(s_B=0\) and make the basis solution and reduced costs recoverable. If no such optimal basis is supplied or reconstructible, basis-specific allowable-cost and right-hand-side ranges cannot be determined from the artifact alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis-dependent postoptimality ranging requires a reconstructible nonsingular optimal basis together with its basis-consistent primal solution, dual solution, and reduced costs; an optimal point alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\)
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The artifact supports basis-dependent postoptimality analysis when the stated optimal-basis identities and feasibility conditions are recoverable.

notation.meaning: Nonsingular submatrix formed from the basic columns.

children.title: Certificate Requirements
children.top_down_role: Method-selection requirements for computational evidence supporting solver conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness certificates for standard-form LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(P=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\\), an accepted certificate must match one of three checkable forms. Optimality is certified by \\(x,y,s\\) with \\(Ax=b\\), \\(x\ge0\\), \\(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\\), \\(s\ge0\\), and \\(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\\). Primal infeasibility is certified by \\(y\\) with \\(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\\) and \\(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\\). If a feasible \\(x^0\\) is supplied, unboundedness is certified by \\(d\\) with \\(Ad=0\\), \\(d\ge0\\), and \\(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\\), because \\(x^0+td\\) is feasible for every \\(t\ge0\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate must provide directly checkable equalities and inequalities proving optimality, primal infeasibility, or an improving feasible ray.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed artifact certifies its corresponding LP status by finite arithmetic checks.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

A specific supporting locator is required.

children.title: Conflict Requirements
children.top_down_role: Method-selection requirements for localized explanations of infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requirements for a constraint subset to constitute an irreducible LP conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite LP constraint system be indexed by \\(I\\), and let \\(F(J)\\) denote the feasible set of the subsystem indexed by \\(J\subseteq I\\). A reported conflict \\(C\subseteq I\\) is valid when \\(F(C)=\varnothing\\). It is irreducible when additionally \\(F(C\setminus\{i\})\ne\varnothing\\) for every \\(i\in C\\). A solver claiming only a conflict need verify the first condition; a solver claiming an irreducible infeasible subsystem must verify both. Constraint identifiers and all bound constraints used by the subsystem must be retained so that these predicates can be checked against the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conflict is an infeasible constraint subset; it is irreducible only when deleting any one member restores feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \\(I\\) is a finite index set of linear equalities, inequalities, and bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(C\\) is an irreducible conflict exactly when \\(F(C)=\varnothing\\) and every single-constraint deletion is feasible.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the subsystem indexed by J.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-system definition of an irreducible infeasible subsystem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conflict and irreducible-conflict conditions are precise and standard, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Certificate–Conflict Interoperability
children.top_down_role: Solver regimes where certificate evidence can or cannot support conflict extraction.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate–Conflict Interoperability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion conditions between algebraic infeasibility certificates and constraint-index conflicts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a linear inequality system as \\(Gx\le h\\). If \\(\lambda\ge0\\), \\(G^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\\), and \\(h^{\mathsf T}\lambda<0\\), then \\(C=\{i:\lambda_i>0\}\\) is a valid conflict because the subsystem indexed by \\(C\\) is infeasible. The support need not be irreducible; deletion filtering is required to obtain an irreducible conflict. Conversely, an infeasible conflict \\(C\\) can be converted into an algebraic certificate only by finding multipliers \\(\lambda_C\ge0\\) satisfying \\(G_C^{\mathsf T}\lambda_C=0\\) and \\(h_C^{\mathsf T}\lambda_C<0\\). Thus interoperability requires preserved row identities, inequality orientations, and multiplier values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas multiplier’s positive support yields a conflict, while converting a conflict back requires solving for valid multipliers; irreducibility is not automatic.
assumptions_latex: \\(G\in\mathbb R^{p\times n},\ h\in\mathbb R^p\\)
All rows use the orientation \\(G_i x\le h_i\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Certificate-to-conflict conversion follows by multiplier support; conflict-to-certificate conversion requires a valid Farkas multiplier on that support.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Farkas-support conversion and warning that support need not be irreducible are mathematically sound, but the record has no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Solution Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-and-gap acceptance test for approximate primal-dual LP solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \\(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\\) and \\(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\\), fix tolerances \\(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g\ge0\\) and positive scaling denominators \\(\beta_p,\beta_d,\beta_g\\). A reported triple \\(x,y,s\\) is acceptable when \\(x\ge-\varepsilon_p\mathbf1\\), \\(s\ge-\varepsilon_d\mathbf1\\), \\(\|Ax-b\|/\beta_p\le\varepsilon_p\\), \\(\|A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\|/\beta_d\le\varepsilon_d\\), and \\( |c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y|/\beta_g\le\varepsilon_g\\). The solver must report the norm, denominators, and tolerances used; otherwise the approximate-solution claim is not reproducible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate acceptance requires declared primal and dual residuals, bound violations, duality gap, norms, scaling denominators, and tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\\)
\\(\beta_p,\beta_d,\beta_g>0\\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reported triple is an approximate primal-dual solution when every stated normalized test passes.

notation.meaning: Declared residual and gap scaling denominators.
