A single scalar tolerance may not represent the multiple feasibility, optimality, and algorithmic tolerances used by an LP solver, and no cited source defines the grid, coupling rule, repetition policy, or stability predicates.

knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Escalation Experiments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled arithmetic-precision escalation for diagnosing numerical instability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose arithmetic precisions \(p_1<\cdots<p_k\) and hold the LP, mathematical algorithm, transformations, tolerances, stopping rules, and resource policy fixed insofar as the implementations permit. At each \(p_i\), solve and independently evaluate the original-coordinate signature \(S_i\) using precision at least \(p_i\). Compare adjacent signatures and certificates. Stop at the first \(p_j\) for which the prescribed agreement predicate holds for two successive precisions, or after \(p_k\). Report the precision trajectory, all implementation differences that could not be held fixed, and whether increased precision resolves, preserves, or changes the original disagreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increase arithmetic precision under controlled settings until two successive diagnostic signatures agree or the precision budget is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: \(p_1<\cdots<p_k\).
Independent validation uses arithmetic precision no lower than the corresponding solve.
Unavoidable implementation changes are recorded.

Validated diagnostic signature at precision i.

Cross-precision algorithm equivalence may be implementation-dependent.

children.title: Seed Variation
children.top_down_role: Controlled runs assessing sensitivity to randomized solver choices.

assumptions_latex: The LP instance, solver version, parameter vector, hardware, thread count, input ordering, and stopping rules are fixed.
The solver exposes an integer seed controlling randomized choices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Differences among recorded outcomes isolate sensitivity to the controlled seed intervention, subject to uncontrolled system noise.

notation.meaning: diagnostic outcome vector from the run using seed s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled intervention on solver randomness, not statistical sampling of LP instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite seed set \(S\), a seed-variation experiment executes the fixed solver configuration once or repeatedly for every \(s\in S\) and records \(Y(s)\), including termination status, objective value, residuals, iteration counts, and runtime. Define the observed seed sensitivity of a scalar diagnostic \(g\) by \[\Delta_{\mathrm{seed}}(g)=\max_{s,t\in S}|g(Y(s))-g(Y(t))|.\] Runs used in this comparison differ only through the seed and unavoidable measurement noise; consequently, nonzero \(\Delta_{\mathrm{seed}}(g)\) is evidence of seed-dependent execution behavior rather than instance variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vary only the solver's random seed, record comparable run outcomes, and measure the range of each diagnostic across seeds.
knowledge_statements.title: Seed Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Seed Variation, but no inspectable citation supports the diagnostic protocol. The claim that nonzero observed range evidences seed-dependent behavior also requires a repetition and noise-separation protocol, since a nonzero range can arise solely from uncontrolled system noise.

children.title: Thread-Count Variation
children.top_down_role: Controlled runs assessing sensitivity to parallel execution width.

assumptions_latex: The LP instance, solver version, parameter vector, hardware allocation, input ordering, seed, and stopping rules are fixed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The experiment separates thread-count sensitivity of numerical and performance diagnostics from changes in the mathematical instance.

finite set of tested positive thread counts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled variation of parallel execution width for one fixed LP configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb{N}_{>0}\), a thread-count variation experiment runs the fixed configuration at every \(p\in P\) and records \(Y(p)\). Numerical sensitivity is measured from status, objective, and residual differences; performance sensitivity is measured from time and resource counters. Relative to a designated baseline \(p_0\in P\), define speedup and efficiency by \[S(p)=\frac{T(p_0)}{T(p)},\qquad E(p)=\frac{S(p)}{p/p_0}.\] Any comparison must retain the same workload and report whether parallel reductions or scheduling can alter the execution path.

children.title: Ordering Variation
children.top_down_role: Controlled runs assessing sensitivity to row, column, or factorization ordering.

assumptions_latex: The LP's mathematical coefficients and all solver settings unrelated to ordering are fixed.

Each result is transformed back to the original row and variable coordinates before comparison. The experiment records status, objective, residuals, iterations, fill, factorization statistics, and runtime. Variation among \(Y(P_r,P_c)\) diagnoses sensitivity to algebraically equivalent input orderings, including ordering-dependent pivoting, presolve, and sparse-factorization behavior.

children.title: Variation-Sensitivity Classification
children.top_down_role: Classification of performance, status, or quality changes across variation experiments.

assumptions_latex: A finite controlled run set and a diagnostic metric with declared equivalence tolerances are available.
Runs are grouped by intervention factor while all other designated factors remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The classification distinguishes reproducible equivalence, performance-only variation, acceptable numerical variation, and consequential variation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based classification of outcomes from controlled execution-variability experiments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For controlled outcomes, classify variation using \(D_{\mathrm{num}}\), \(D_{\mathrm{perf}}\), and declared tolerances. The class is reproducibly equivalent when \(D_{\mathrm{num}}\leq\tau_{\mathrm{num}}\) and \(D_{\mathrm{perf}}\leq\tau_{\mathrm{perf}}\); performance-sensitive when \(D_{\mathrm{num}}\leq\tau_{\mathrm{num}}\) but \(D_{\mathrm{perf}}>\tau_{\mathrm{perf}}\); numerically sensitive when termination status agrees and certified feasibility and optimality conditions remain satisfied, but \(D_{\mathrm{num}}>\tau_{\mathrm{num}}\); and consequentially sensitive when status differs or any run violates the declared certificate tolerances. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify controlled-run differences as equivalent, performance-sensitive, numerically sensitive, or consequential using declared metrics, tolerances, and certificate checks.

assumptions_latex: A solver phase forms or updates sparse factors of a basis or Newton-system matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational cost regime for sparse simplex and interior-point linear algebra.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8, §1, Solving Systems of Equations: LU-Factorization, p. 124

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) denote the measured arithmetic work of factor construction or update, \(M_F\) the factor storage, and \(R\) the measured work of all other operations in the same solver phase. The phase is factorization-dominated when \(F>R\), with the stronger asymptotic designation \(R=o(F)\) for an instance family. For dense factorization of an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(F=\Theta(n^3)\) and \(M_F=\Theta(n^2)\); for sparse factors, both quantities depend on fill, ordering, and pivoting and therefore must be reported from the realized factors rather than inferred solely from \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factorization dominates when building or updating matrix factors costs more than all other phase operations; sparse cost depends on realized fill and pivoting.
knowledge_statements.title: Factorization-Dominated Costs

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 8, §1, Solving Systems of Equations: LU-Factorization, p. 124

assumptions_latex: The dominant iteration kernels are sparse matrix-vector products with fixed matrix sparsity during the measured phase.
Costs count arithmetic work and transferred data under a stated sparse storage format.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is matrix-vector-dominated when accumulated sparse products exceed all other measured work.

notation.meaning: number of nonzeros of the matrix

review_flags: sparse iterative LP solver source needed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost model for LP methods whose repeated sparse products dominate execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(k\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}\) be the number of products by \(A\) or \(A^{\mathsf T}\). Conventional sparse storage gives arithmetic work \[W_{\mathrm{mv}}=\Theta\!\left(k\operatorname{nnz}(A)\right)\] and storage \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)\). The measured phase is matrix-vector-dominated when \(W_{\mathrm{mv}}>R\), where \(R\) is the aggregate work of all other kernels; asymptotically, the designation requires \(R=o(W_{\mathrm{mv}})\). Because sparse products commonly have low arithmetic intensity, elapsed time must also be assessed against memory traffic rather than predicted from the operation count alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated sparse matrix-vector products cost linearly in their count and matrix nonzeros; they dominate when their accumulated cost exceeds all other kernels.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix–Vector-Dominated Costs

children.title: Memory-Traffic Costs
children.top_down_role: Costs associated with moving solver data through the memory hierarchy.

assumptions_latex: A solver execution is partitioned into kernels with measured or modeled data transfers between specified memory levels.
Transferred bytes include matrix values, indices, vectors, factors, and write allocation where applicable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The traffic lower bound yields a bandwidth-based time bound and identifies traffic-heavy kernels.

notation.meaning: bytes transferred across a selected memory interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bandwidth cost model at a declared level of the memory hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a declared memory interface, let \(Q\) be the total bytes transferred by a solver kernel and \(B\) its attainable sustained bandwidth. Irrespective of arithmetic throughput, the kernel time satisfies \[T\geq \frac{Q}{B}.\] For a sequence of kernels, traffic is counted at the chosen interface without double-counting transfers internal to lower levels. A memory-traffic cost report specifies the interface, storage formats, cache state convention, read and write volumes, and repetitions. A kernel is traffic-dominated only when this bandwidth bound is tighter than the corresponding compute-throughput bound and is consistent with measured counters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count bytes crossing a specified memory interface; transferred bytes divided by sustained bandwidth lower-bounds runtime and diagnoses traffic-heavy kernels.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Traffic Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bandwidth lower bound and reporting requirements fit Memory-Traffic Costs and are stated with the necessary interface qualification. No inspectable computer-architecture or performance-model source is supplied, so the bound's interpretation and the traffic-dominance criterion remain unsupported.

children.title: Storage Costs
children.top_down_role: Memory-capacity costs for model data, factors, iterates, and auxiliary state.

assumptions_latex: The solver's sparse matrices, vectors, factors, metadata, and workspaces are represented using declared numeric and index types.
Peak simultaneously live allocations define the memory requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sum of live object sizes determines peak storage and feasibility under a memory capacity limit.

notation.meaning: byte size of live object j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak-capacity model for solver data structures, distinct from memory traffic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At time \(t\), let \(L(t)\) be the set of live solver objects and let \(M_j\) include the values, indices, alignment, and allocator overhead of object \(j\). Peak storage is \[M_{\mathrm{peak}}=\max_t\sum_{j\in L(t)}M_j.\] Execution is capacity-feasible only if \(M_{\mathrm{peak}}\leq C\), where \(C\) is the usable memory limit. For a sparse matrix, storage is proportional to its stored values and indices, whereas factor storage is governed by realized fill. A diagnostic must report temporary workspaces and concurrent copies; summing only persistent input arrays is not a valid peak estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Peak storage is the largest sum of simultaneously live allocations, including indices, factor fill, temporary workspaces, copies, and allocator overhead.
knowledge_statements.title: Storage Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The peak-live-allocation formula fits Storage Costs and correctly distinguishes capacity from traffic. The sparse-storage, factor-fill, allocator-overhead, and feasibility claims have no inspectable citation and therefore cannot yet be accepted as candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Memory-Hierarchy Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Performance regimes dominated by cache behavior, bandwidth, or data locality.

assumptions_latex: For each solver kernel, operation count, transferred bytes, elapsed time, and relevant cache or bandwidth counters are measured consistently.
Peak or sustained compute and bandwidth rates are specified for the tested hardware.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A memory-hierarchy bottleneck is diagnosed only when traffic bounds and measurements jointly exclude compute throughput as the active limit.

notation.meaning: arithmetic operations divided by transferred bytes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic predicate combining arithmetic intensity, bandwidth bounds, and observed counters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For work \(W\), traffic \(Q\), arithmetic intensity \(I=W/Q\), compute rate \(P\), and bandwidth \(B\), the idealized execution time obeys \[T\geq\max\left\{\frac{W}{P},\frac{Q}{B}\right\}.\] A kernel is classified as bottlenecked at the selected memory level when \(Q/B\geq W/P\), measured bandwidth approaches the attainable \(B\), and increasing arithmetic throughput does not materially reduce time. Cache-miss, latency, nonuniform-memory, or capacity bottlenecks require corresponding counters or controlled placement experiments; low arithmetic intensity alone is insufficient to identify the responsible hierarchy level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagnose a hierarchy bottleneck when the bandwidth bound dominates the compute bound and measurements corroborate the responsible memory level.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Hierarchy Bottlenecks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Memory-Hierarchy Bottlenecks and appropriately states that low arithmetic intensity alone does not localize a bottleneck. An authoritative roofline and hardware-counter source is required to support the idealized bound and the proposed classification criteria.

assumptions_latex: The same fixed workload is executed with different positive processor counts on comparable hardware allocations.
Elapsed times include a declared policy for initialization, synchronization, communication, and serial work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Speedup and efficiency quantify scalability, while the serial fraction imposes an upper bound on attainable speedup.

notation.meaning: elapsed time using p processing units
fraction of baseline work that is effectively serial

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-scaling cost model for fixed LP solver workloads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed workload, define speedup \(S_p=T_1/T_p\), efficiency \(E_p=S_p/p\), and parallel overhead \(O_p=pT_p-T_1\). Under the serial-fraction model with \(0\leq f\leq1\), attainable speedup satisfies \[S_p\leq\frac{1}{f+(1-f)/p},\] and hence \(\limsup_{p\to\infty}S_p\leq1/f\) when \(f>0\). Solver scalability costs include synchronization, communication, load imbalance, duplicated work, and memory-bandwidth contention. Reported scaling comparisons must preserve the instance and stopping rule and must state whether setup, presolve, factorization, and output are included in \(T_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed work, report speedup, efficiency, and overhead; serial work, communication, imbalance, and bandwidth contention limit scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Scalability Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-scaling quantities and serial-fraction bound fit Parallel Scalability Costs and are mathematically consistent. No parallel-performance citation is supplied for Amdahl's model, overhead accounting, or the stated reporting protocol.

assumptions_latex: A solver run at tolerance parameter \(\varepsilon>0\) returns diagnostics and incurs measured cost \(C(\varepsilon)\).
Accuracy is evaluated by declared normalized primal, dual, gap, or certificate residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nondominated accuracy-cost pairs form the empirical tradeoff frontier; tighter tolerance is justified only by the accuracy it actually delivers.

notation.meaning: aggregate declared accuracy error at tolerance epsilon
measured computational cost at tolerance epsilon

review_flags: empirical frontier formulation extends textbook discussion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical Pareto formulation for termination accuracy versus solver resource use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For tested tolerances \(E\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}\), associate each successful run with \((C(\varepsilon),R(\varepsilon))\). A pair at \(\varepsilon\in E\) is dominated if some \(\eta\in E\) satisfies \(C(\eta)\leq C(\varepsilon)\) and \(R(\eta)\leq R(\varepsilon)\), with at least one strict inequality. The nondominated pairs constitute the empirical accuracy-cost frontier. Comparisons must use identical instances, scaling conventions, hardware, and stopping diagnostics. Requested tolerance is not itself achieved accuracy: conclusions use measured residuals and certificates, and runs with incorrect status or failed certificates remain failures rather than favorable low-cost points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare measured cost with achieved residuals, retain nondominated pairs, and never treat a requested tolerance as evidence of attained accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy–Cost Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empirical Pareto construction is precise and relevant to Accuracy–Cost Tradeoffs, but the sole citation is a general performance-tradeoffs section and the candidate itself states that the frontier formulation extends that discussion. Full-text support for the Pareto definition and treatment of failed runs is therefore insufficient.

children.title: Instance-Set Design
children.top_down_role: Selection, grouping, and coverage of LP instances used in evaluation.

assumptions_latex: A benchmark targets a declared solver population, LP feature space, and use case.
Every selected instance has immutable data, provenance, licensing, and integrity metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid instance set supports reproducible, stratified aggregation without allowing solver outcomes to influence membership.

notation.meaning: predeclared strata partitioning the target population
predeclared weight assigned to instance i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Design predicate for reproducible LP solver benchmark instance sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance-set design specifies a finite set \(\mathcal{I}=\bigcup_{h=1}^H\mathcal{I}_h\), where the strata \(\mathcal{I}_h\) are disjoint and defined before solver outcomes are observed. Inclusion and exclusion predicates, deduplication rules, versioned instance hashes, provenance, train-versus-test separation, and weights \(w_i\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}w_i=1\) are fixed in the benchmark protocol. The set is fit for comparison only if it covers the declared target features, prevents outcome-dependent selection, and permits every reported aggregate to be reconstructed from per-instance results using the declared strata and weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Predeclare representative strata, membership rules, hashes, provenance, deduplication, and weights so benchmark aggregates are reproducible and free of outcome-based selection.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Set Design

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Instance-Set Design and gives a coherent reproducibility protocol, but its representativeness, stratification, outcome-independent selection, train-test separation, and weighting requirements are substantive benchmark-design claims without an inspectable source.

children.title: Performance-Metric Design
children.top_down_role: Selection of time, resource, robustness, and solution-quality measures.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark instance set \(P\) and solver set \(S\) are finite and nonempty.
Every run uses a fixed resource limit and a declared success predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting metric vector permits separate comparison of efficiency, reliability, and returned-solution accuracy without treating an unsuccessful run as an ordinary finite observation.

notation.meaning: Measured resource consumption for instance p and solver s
Indicator that the declared success predicate is satisfied
Vector of primal, dual, and complementarity residual measures

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a multi-component benchmark metric rather than a single runtime score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \((p,s)\in P\times S\), a performance record is the tuple \(M_{p,s}=(q_{p,s},t_{p,s},e_{p,s})\), where \(q_{p,s}\in\{0,1\}\), \(t_{p,s}\in[0,\infty]\), and \(e_{p,s}\in[0,\infty]^k\). The measurement protocol must specify the resource represented by \(t_{p,s}\), the residual scaling used in \(e_{p,s}\), the stopping tolerance, and the treatment of limits and failures. Aggregate statistics must report success frequency separately from conditional resource and accuracy summaries over \(\{(p,s):q_{p,s}=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Record success, resource use, and numerical accuracy separately, with explicit scaling, limits, and aggregation rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Performance-Metric Design

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit Performance-Metric Design, but the cited locator is only visible as a table-of-contents entry and concerns general simplex performance measures. It does not inspectably support the proposed success-resource-residual tuple, failure treatment, or aggregation requirements. A benchmarking source addressing numerical accuracy and unsuccessful runs is required.

children.title: Instance–Metric Alignment
children.top_down_role: Alignment between benchmark population characteristics and reported evaluation metrics.

assumptions_latex: Each instance has declared structural attributes and an independently checkable solution-status class.
Every reported metric has a stated scientific question and aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each aggregate is computed only over its declared domain, so the reported comparison cannot silently substitute easy-instance speed for broad robustness or infeasible-instance detection.

notation.meaning: Domain of instances on which metric j is meaningful
Metric evaluated for instance p and solver s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires every metric to match the instance classes and claims it can validly assess.

source_refs.locator: 5. Empirical Average Performance of the Simplex Method p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance-metric design is aligned when every metric \(m_j\) has an explicit domain \(D_j\subseteq P\), every stratum relevant to the intended claim is represented in \(D_j\), and undefined observations are recorded as such rather than assigned favorable numerical values. If \(m_j\) concerns optimal-solution accuracy, then \(D_j\) contains only instances with the applicable reference status; if it concerns infeasibility detection, then its domain includes independently certified infeasible instances. Aggregation weights over \(D_j\) must be fixed before solver outcomes are examined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric is aligned when its domain, instance strata, missing-value rules, and weights match the claim being evaluated.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance–Metric Alignment

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Empirical Average Performance of the Simplex Method p. 50

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Instance–Metric Alignment and is internally coherent, but the cited section on empirical average simplex performance does not inspectably support the stronger requirements concerning metric domains, certified status strata, undefined observations, and outcome-independent weighting.

assumptions_latex: All solvers are run on the same instances under comparable resource limits.
A common feasibility and optimality qualification rule is applied to every returned result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solver can receive a finite performance value only after meeting the common accuracy requirement; thus faster but insufficiently accurate outputs do not dominate qualified outputs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies a common numerical-accuracy gate before comparing solver resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_{p,s}\) be the maximum of consistently scaled primal-feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity or objective-gap residuals appropriate to instance \(p\). For a fixed tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), define \[T_{p,s}^{(\varepsilon)}=\begin{cases}t_{p,s},&E_{p,s}\leq\varepsilon\text{ and the reported status is correct},\\ +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Performance comparisons at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) must use \(T_{p,s}^{(\varepsilon)}\), disclose the scaling in \(E_{p,s}\), and report qualification rates alongside summaries of finite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare resource use only after each result passes the same status and numerical-accuracy checks; report qualification rates separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Qualified Performance Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits Accuracy-Qualified Performance Comparison, and the displayed definition is properly delimited. The cited implementation-performance locator does not inspectably establish the common residual gate, infinite penalty, status-correctness requirement, or qualification-rate reporting. A source on accuracy-qualified solver benchmarking is needed.

children.title: Solver-Configuration Capture
children.top_down_role: Recording of solver parameters, presets, and enabled features.

assumptions_latex: The solver exposes effective parameter values after defaults, presets, and automatic choices are resolved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two runs have identical captured solver configurations exactly when their canonical effective-configuration maps and run-control policies agree.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reproducible experiments require effective parameter and policy capture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Captures effective settings, including defaults and automatic policies, rather than only user overrides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solver-configuration capture represents a run by a canonical map \(C:K\to\bigcup_{k\in K}V_k\) with \(C(k)\in V_k\) for every behavior-affecting parameter \(k\). The record includes algorithm selection, presolve and scaling policies, tolerances, pricing or ordering rules, crossover, numerical safeguards, thread count, random seed, resource limits, and stopping rules. Values inherited from defaults or presets are recorded as effective values, while unresolved automatic choices are accompanied by the rule and information needed to reconstruct their resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store every effective solver setting and run-control policy, including defaults, automatic choices, seeds, threads, tolerances, and limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Configuration Capture

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate kind for Solver-Configuration Capture, but no source supports the asserted exhaustive field set, canonical effective-configuration requirement, or reconstruction rule for automatic choices. Standard-field rationale alone is insufficient for this detailed candidate.

children.title: Execution-Environment Capture
children.top_down_role: Recording of hardware, operating system, libraries, and runtime conditions.

assumptions_latex: The measured run executes within a well-defined software and hardware environment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The captured environment identifies the external conditions under which resource measurements and numerical behavior were observed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resource measurements depend on software, hardware, and runtime environment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the environment fields needed to interpret timing and numerical variability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Execution-environment capture represents a run by a canonical record \(E=\{(f,E(f)):f\in F\}\). The field set \(F\) includes processor model, available memory, accelerator if used, operating system, architecture, compiler and numerical-library identities, thread-affinity policy, container or virtual-machine description, environment variables affecting computation, and the resource-measurement method. For shared or dynamically managed systems, the record also states allocation constraints and concurrency conditions relevant to elapsed time or memory consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Record the hardware, operating system, libraries, runtime controls, allocation conditions, and measurement method affecting observed behavior.
knowledge_statements.title: Execution-Environment Capture

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits Execution-Environment Capture, but the detailed mandatory field set and claims about shared-system allocation and concurrency conditions have no cited reproducibility or benchmarking source.

children.title: Version Capture
children.top_down_role: Recording of solver, dependency, model, and benchmark-suite versions.

assumptions_latex: Solver behavior may depend on executable, source, model, library, and benchmark revisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The version record uniquely identifies, or cryptographically binds, every mutable artifact required to reconstruct the evaluated run.

notation.meaning: Recorded version identifier for artifact a
Cryptographic digest of artifact a when available

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reproducibility requires immutable identification of mutable artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires immutable identification of all solver, dependency, model, and benchmark artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Version capture is complete for a run when every behavior-affecting artifact \(a\in A\) has a recorded identifier \(v(a)\), and every locally built or mutable artifact additionally has a digest \(h(a)\). The set \(A\) includes the solver executable or source revision, build configuration, linked numerical libraries, modeling interface, input converter, benchmark instance revision, and evaluation scripts. A mutable branch name, package label without build metadata, or unqualified term such as “latest” does not constitute a version identifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identify every mutable solver, dependency, model, benchmark, and evaluation artifact by an immutable version or digest.
knowledge_statements.title: Version Capture

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is defensible because the statement characterizes completeness of version capture, but no source supports the proposed artifact scope, digest requirement, or rejection of particular identifier forms. An authoritative reproducibility source is required.

children.title: Reproduction-Metadata Completeness
children.top_down_role: Coverage checks for metadata required to interpret or reproduce benchmark results.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark instance and raw run outcome are retained or immutably identified.
Reproduction means rerunning the same experimental protocol, not necessarily obtaining bitwise-identical output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A metadata record is complete only if no unrecorded experimental choice remains that can change qualification, measured performance, or the declared equivalence of reproduced outcomes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: completeness is defined relative to all behavior- and interpretation-affecting fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines completeness relative to reconstruction of both execution and result interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reproduction record \(R\) is complete when \(F_{\mathrm{req}}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(R)\), where \(F_{\mathrm{req}}\) contains immutable instance identification, effective solver configuration, execution environment, artifact versions, command and input transformations, seed and concurrency controls, resource limits, measurement protocol, success and accuracy predicates, failure policy, aggregation rule, and outcome-equivalence criterion. Each field must be machine-readable or unambiguously interpretable, and referenced external artifacts must be content-addressed or archived.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metadata is complete when it reconstructs the run, measurement, qualification, failure handling, aggregation, and outcome-equivalence rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Reproduction-Metadata Completeness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Reproduction-Metadata Completeness, but the comprehensive required-field set, content-addressing requirement, and machine-readability criterion are unsupported by any citation.

children.title: Deterministic Runs
children.top_down_role: Repeatable solver behavior under fixed inputs, configuration, execution environment, plus controlled resources.

assumptions_latex: The instance, effective configuration, executable artifacts, execution environment, and initial state are fixed.
The declared observation map and outcome-equivalence relation are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated runs under the fixed inputs belong to one declared equivalence class; otherwise the regime is not deterministic at that observation level.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: determinism is single-valued behavior relative to fixed inputs and an observation equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines determinism relative to a declared observation level, from status equivalence to bitwise identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A run regime is deterministic relative to observation map \(Y\) and equivalence relation \(\sim\) if, for every admissible fixed input \(z\), all repeated executions \(r_1,r_2\) satisfy \(Y(z,r_1)\sim Y(z,r_2)\). The input \(z\) includes the instance, effective solver configuration, versions, environment, initial state, and all scheduling or seed information treated as controlled. Bitwise determinism uses equality for \(\sim\); numerical determinism may instead use equality of status and prescribed tolerances for objective values and residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is deterministic when repeated executions with all controlled inputs fixed produce equivalent outcomes under a declared criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Runs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct role for Deterministic Runs, but no authoritative source is supplied. The notation entry defines the outcome as Y(z), whereas the statement uses Y(z,r); the execution variable r and its domain are not formally introduced. Source-backed clarification of the observation model is required.

children.title: Nondeterministic Runs
children.top_down_role: Run-to-run variation arising from parallel execution, randomized choices, scheduling, or unstable numerical paths.

assumptions_latex: At least one behavior-affecting input or event is uncontrolled or intentionally randomized.
The controlled run context is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reproducible evaluation of the regime requires repeated trials and distributional summaries rather than a single run treated as invariant.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nondeterministic computation is represented by a nondegenerate conditional outcome distribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats repeated-run outcomes as a conditional distribution rather than one fixed value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A run regime is nondeterministic relative to an outcome-equivalence relation \(\sim\) when there exists a controlled context \(z\) such that \(Y(z,\omega)\) occupies more than one \(\sim\)-equivalence class as the uncontrolled state \(\omega\) varies with positive probability. Its performance object is therefore the conditional distribution \(\mathcal{L}(Y\mid z)\), including failure probability, rather than one observation. A benchmark summary must specify the sampling unit, number of repetitions, seed policy when applicable, and distributional statistic or interval reported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondeterministic regime has multiple possible outcome classes under fixed controls and must be evaluated through repeated-run distributions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondeterministic Runs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits Nondeterministic Runs, but the probability law or probability space governing omega is not introduced even though positive probability and the conditional law are essential to the claim. No source supports the definition or the prescribed repetition and reporting requirements.

children.title: Sources of Run Variability
children.top_down_role: Implementation, platform, configuration, plus workload factors that can alter observed solver behavior.

assumptions_latex: A run outcome is determined by controlled inputs together with possibly uncontrolled runtime state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Observed variability can be attributed only relative to the declared partition between controlled factors and residual state; omitted factors remain confounded with residual variability.

notation.meaning: Observed status, accuracy, and resource outcome
Instance, configuration, environment, and version tuple

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: outcome variability is factored into controlled experimental variables and residual state
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Organizes variability into instance, configuration, environment, version, and residual runtime contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run outcomes admit the experimental representation \(Y=F(I,C,E,V,\omega)\), where \(I\) is the instance and input encoding, \(C\) the effective solver configuration, \(E\) the execution environment, \(V\) the artifact-version tuple, and \(\omega\) residual runtime state. Components of \(\omega\) may include random-number state, thread scheduling, reduction order, concurrent load, memory placement, and dynamic frequency changes. A variability claim must state which components are fixed, randomized, blocked, or unobserved and must not attribute variation to one component when the experimental design confounds it with another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model outcomes as depending on instance, configuration, environment, versions, and residual runtime state, while explicitly identifying confounding.
knowledge_statements.title: Sources of Run Variability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits Sources of Run Variability, but writing Y=F(I,C,E,V,omega) asserts a deterministic structural representation that is not justified by the assumptions or a source. The listed variability factors and the experimental-confounding rule also require authoritative support.

children.title: Reproducibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on exact replication across machines, thread counts, libraries, solver builds, or execution conditions.

assumptions_latex: The reproduction claim declares controlled fields, admissible perturbations, observables, and an outcome-equivalence relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The claim extends only across contexts in \(B\); behavior outside \(B\) is not certified by successful reproduction within it.

notation.meaning: Set of contexts covered by the reproduction claim

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reproducibility claims require an explicit domain and equivalence criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds every reproducibility claim by admissible contexts, observables, and outcome equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reproducibility boundary is a declared set \(B\) of admissible run contexts together with an equivalence relation \(\sim\) on observed outcomes. A claim of reproduction from reference context \(z_0\in B\) requires \(Y(z)\sim Y(z_0)\) for contexts \(z\in B\) selected by the stated repetition protocol. Changing an unquantified field, crossing to \(z\notin B\), or examining an observable excluded from \(Y\) invalidates the inference, even when instance and solver names are unchanged. Statistical reproduction additionally specifies the distributional distance and acceptance threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reproducibility claim is valid only within its declared contexts, observables, equivalence criterion, and statistical acceptance rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Reproducibility Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the appropriate kind for Reproducibility Boundaries, but no source supports this formalization. The requirement applies only to contexts selected by an unspecified repetition protocol, so it does not clearly quantify which members of B must satisfy outcome equivalence.

children.title: Performance Profile Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Reading relative solver coverage, performance ratios, dominance regions, plus benchmark-wide trends.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark instance set \(P\) and solver set \(S\) are finite and nonempty.
Each performance value uses one declared accuracy and failure policy, with at least one finite value per instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordinate measures the fraction of instances solved within factor \(\tau\) of the best recorded solver; its limiting value is the solver's success fraction under the declared policy.

notation.meaning: Performance value for instance p and solver s
Ratio to the best finite performance on instance p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard finite-benchmark profile with unsuccessful runs assigned infinite ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(p\in P\), define \(r_{p,s}=t_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}t_{p,u}\) when \(t_{p,s}<+\infty\), and \(r_{p,s}=+\infty\) otherwise. The performance profile is \[\rho_s(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] Thus \(\rho_s(1)\) is the fraction on which \(s\) attains the best recorded value, \(\rho_s(\tau)\) is its fraction within factor \(\tau\) of the best, and \(\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\rho_s(\tau)\) is its finite-outcome fraction under the fixed failure policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile gives the fraction of instances where a solver is within a factor of the best; its limit gives the success fraction.
knowledge_statements.title: Performance Profile Interpretation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is suitable for interpreting a performance profile, but the canonical performance-profile source is absent. The assumptions do not require positive performance values, so the ratio can be undefined when the per-instance minimum is zero. The formula also omits an explicit definition for a finite numerator when the minimum is not a valid positive finite value. These details must be corrected against the canonical source before acceptance.

children.title: Failure Category Accounting
children.top_down_role: Classification of limits, crashes, invalid results, numerical failures, plus unresolved outcomes in benchmark summaries.

assumptions_latex: A finite benchmark set \(P\) and solver set \(S\) are fixed.
Each run \((p,s)\in P\times S\) has exactly one terminal label in a declared finite category set \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The category counts form a complete, nonoverlapping accounting of all benchmark runs.

notation.meaning: Number of runs assigned category k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting applies after a benchmark protocol fixes mutually exclusive terminal categories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa:P\times S\to K\) assign every run exactly one terminal category, such as reliable success, time limit, memory exhaustion, numerical failure, or other declared failure. Define \(N_k=\lvert\{(p,s)\in P\times S:\kappa(p,s)=k\}\rvert\) and \(N=\lvert P\rvert\lvert S\rvert\). Valid failure-category accounting requires \(N_k\geq 0\) for every \(k\in K\), pairwise disjoint category preimages, and \(\sum_{k\in K}N_k=N\). Any run lacking a category, or assigned multiple categories, invalidates the accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every benchmark run receives one terminal category; category counts must be disjoint, nonnegative, and sum to the total number of runs.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Category Accounting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no inspectable source supports the benchmark-category protocol.

children.title: Censored Run Treatment
children.top_down_role: Scope of timeout, memory-limit, interrupted, or otherwise incomplete runs within reported evidence.

assumptions_latex: For each problem \(p\), at least one solver produces a reliable finite reference performance value.
A declared policy specifies how right-censored runs are represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Censored observations are excluded from ordinary finite ratios unless the declared policy supplies a policy-dependent surrogate ratio.

notation.meaning: Best reliable uncensored performance on problem p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-censoring covers runs stopped before a reliable performance value is observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an uncensored reliable run, set \(r_{p,s}^{\pi}=t_{p,s}/t_p^*\), where \(t_p^*=\min\{t_{p,u}:u\in S\text{ has a reliable uncensored run on }p\}\). If a run is right-censored at limit \(L_{p,s}\), record the observation as \(t_{p,s}>L_{p,s}\), not as the equality \(t_{p,s}=L_{p,s}\). A declared policy \(\pi\) may map that observation to \(+\infty\) or to a stated finite penalty, but the mapping and censoring threshold must accompany the resulting profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stopped run is recorded as exceeding its limit. Any infinite or penalized performance ratio must be explicitly declared as policy-dependent.
knowledge_statements.title: Censored Run Treatment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits censored-run treatment, but the proposed censoring and penalty conventions require an inspectable performance-profile source.

children.title: Profile Sensitivity to Failure Policies
children.top_down_role: Changes in comparative conclusions caused by penalties, exclusions, category mappings, or denominator choices.

assumptions_latex: Two declared failure policies \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\) are applied to the same run records.
Their performance profiles use the same benchmark and solver sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Profile differences are exactly determined by runs whose assigned ratios or admissibility differ between the policies.

notation.meaning: Runs treated differently by the two policies

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity compares profiles computed from identical raw runs under different failure policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\rho_s^{\pi}(\tau)=|P|^{-1}\lvert\{p\in P:r_{p,s}^{\pi}\leq\tau\}\rvert\) for \(\tau\geq1\), and let \(D_s(\pi,\pi')=\{p:r_{p,s}^{\pi}\neq r_{p,s}^{\pi'}\}\). Then \(\bigl|\rho_s^{\pi}(\tau)-\rho_s^{\pi'}(\tau)\bigr|\leq |D_s(\pi,\pi')|/|P|\) for every \(\tau\geq1\). Hence policies agreeing on every run yield identical profiles, while any reported sensitivity must be traceable to changed ratios, eligibility, or failure classifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing failure policy can alter a solver profile only through runs whose ratios or eligibility change; the affected-run fraction bounds the change.
knowledge_statements.title: Profile Sensitivity to Failure Policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affected-problem bound is correct under the stated fixed-denominator profile definition, but no source supports the performance-profile convention or policy comparison.

children.title: Time Limit Without a Reliable Solution

assumptions_latex: A run is terminated when elapsed resource time reaches a declared limit \(T\).
Reliability is judged by a declared certificate predicate \(R(z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination at the limit without a certificate satisfying \(R\) is an operational failure, not evidence of an LP status.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary separates resource termination from certified mathematical termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A run belongs to the time-limit-without-reliable-solution regime when its stopping time satisfies \(t\geq T\) and either no candidate result \(z\) is returned or \(R(z)=\mathrm{false}\). The event certifies only that the computational budget was exhausted. It does not certify optimality, primal infeasibility, dual infeasibility, or unboundedness. Any incumbent objective, residual, or bound may be retained as diagnostic evidence, but it must not be reported as a reliable solution unless it satisfies the predeclared predicate \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reaching the time limit without a result passing declared reliability checks is a resource failure and establishes no mathematical LP status.
knowledge_statements.title: Time Limit Without a Reliable Solution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and distinction between resource exhaustion and mathematical status are appropriate, but the reliability semantics lack cited support.

children.title: Memory Capacity Exhaustion
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by insufficient process, system, device, or address-space capacity during solver execution.

assumptions_latex: A solver run has an enforceable memory capacity \(M\).
Its live allocated memory at time \(t\) is \(m(t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A failed allocation required to continue establishes memory-capacity exhaustion but no mathematical status for the LP.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity exhaustion concerns the entire solver process, not a particular numerical workspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Memory-capacity exhaustion occurs at time \(t\) when continuation requires an allocation of size \(a(t)>0\), the available-capacity condition \(m(t)+a(t)\leq M\) fails, and the solver cannot recover by releasing optional storage or using an admissible alternative representation. The event is operational: it identifies insufficient memory under the recorded platform and configuration. Unless an independent valid certificate was completed before the failed allocation, the event establishes neither feasibility nor infeasibility, boundedness, unboundedness, or optimality of the LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory exhaustion occurs when a required allocation exceeds available capacity and no admissible recovery succeeds; it does not determine the LP's status.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory Capacity Exhaustion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits the operational failure boundary, but the capacity and recovery model is platform-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Factorization Workspace Exhaustion
children.top_down_role: Failures tied to inadequate workspace or storage during basis and linear-system factorization.

assumptions_latex: A linear-system factorization requires workspace beyond its persistent matrix storage.
The implementation exposes a workspace limit \(W\) or a failed workspace allocation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exceeding factorization workspace is a factorization failure even when total process capacity has not otherwise been exhausted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary applies to sparse linear-system factorizations used inside an LP solver.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8, Section 1, Solving Systems of Equations: \(LU\)-Factorization, p. 124

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matrix \(A\) and factorization strategy \(\sigma\), let \(w(A,\sigma)\) denote the temporary and dynamically growing workspace required to complete the factorization. Factorization-workspace exhaustion occurs when \(w(A,\sigma)>W\), or when a required workspace allocation fails, before usable factors are produced. This category is distinct from general memory-capacity exhaustion when other process memory remains available but the factorization workspace is capped, fragmented, or represented by bounded index structures. It certifies failure of that factorization attempt, not failure of every possible ordering or linear solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorization attempt exhausts workspace when its required temporary or growing storage exceeds the available workspace, without ruling out alternative factorizations.
knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Workspace Exhaustion

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 8, Section 1, Solving Systems of Equations: \(LU\)-Factorization, p. 124

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited LU-factorization section is relevant background but does not demonstrably support the specific workspace-cap, fragmentation, bounded-index, and alternative-factorization claims.

children.title: Fill-In Growth Pressure
children.top_down_role: Memory escalation associated with sparsity loss, ordering effects, or unexpectedly dense factors.

assumptions_latex: A sparse factorization of \(A\) produces factors collected as \(F\).
Storage is measured by the number of structurally stored entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Large fill ratio predicts factor-storage pressure relative to the original sparse matrix, but is not itself an exhaustion event.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fill pressure is a structural diagnostic for sparse factorization memory demand.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8, Section 1, Solving Systems of Equations: \(LU\)-Factorization, p. 124

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the fill ratio by \(\phi=\operatorname{nnz}(F)/\max\{1,\operatorname{nnz}(A)\}\), using a declared convention for counting factor entries. Increasing \(\phi\) increases factor-storage demand relative to input storage and may cause workspace or memory exhaustion. However, \(\phi\) alone is not an exhaustion certificate: exhaustion additionally requires a capacity violation or failed allocation. Because ordering, pivoting, scaling, and numerical thresholds can change \(F\), comparisons of fill pressure are meaningful only when those choices and the counting convention are recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fill ratio measures factor entries relative to input entries. High fill indicates memory pressure but proves exhaustion only with a capacity violation.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill-In Growth Pressure

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 8, Section 1, Solving Systems of Equations: \(LU\)-Factorization, p. 124

children.title: Exhaustion Diagnostic Evidence
children.top_down_role: Logs, resource measurements, factorization reports, plus termination records relevant to exhaustion classification.

assumptions_latex: The platform can report allocation failures and resource limits.
The solver can identify its current computational phase.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The captured tuple is a reproducible diagnostic certificate of the observed exhaustion event, not a certificate of the LP's mathematical status.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evidence distinguishes process-capacity, factorization-workspace, and fill-driven exhaustion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exhaustion evidence record is \(E=(M,m_{\max},a_f,q,\phi,\sigma,e)\), where \(M\) is the applicable capacity, \(m_{\max}\) peak memory, \(a_f\) the failed requested allocation, \(q\) the solver phase, \(\phi\) the latest fill ratio when applicable, \(\sigma\) the ordering and factorization configuration, and \(e\) the platform or solver error code. The record supports an exhaustion classification only if \(e\) denotes allocation or workspace failure and the recorded capacity semantics make the failed request checkable. Missing fields must be marked unavailable rather than inferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reproducible exhaustion record includes capacity, peak use, failed request, solver phase, fill, factorization settings, and the original error code.
knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustion Diagnostic Evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A certificate is an appropriate role for this evidence tuple, but the proposed minimum fields and their platform semantics are uncited and nonstandardized.

children.title: Numerical Error Signatures
children.top_down_role: Observable solver messages, residual anomalies, unstable progress, or invalid numerical output associated with numerical failure.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Error Signatures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These signatures invalidate unconditional acceptance of a returned optimal label but do not, by themselves, identify the underlying cause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the LP \(\min\{c^T x:Ax=b,\ x\geq 0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For a returned triple \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\), let \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^Ty+s-c\), and \(r_c=Xs\). A numerical status-reliability signature is present if a component of \((x,y,s,r_p,r_d,r_c)\) is nonfinite, an arithmetic or factorization error is reported, or a returned optimal label is accompanied by \(\lVert r_p\rVert>\varepsilon_p\), \(\lVert r_d\rVert>\varepsilon_d\), or \(\lVert r_c\rVert>\varepsilon_c\) under the declared norms and scaling. Such a signature prevents unconditional acceptance of that label unless an independent valid certificate is available; excessive residuals alone do not determine whether the cause was numerical failure, premature termination, or lack of convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonfinite quantities and reported arithmetic or factorization errors are numerical warning signatures. Residuals exceeding declared tolerances invalidate unconditional acceptance of a claimed optimal status but do not alone identify the cause.
assumptions_latex: The LP data satisfy \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The returned variables satisfy \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\).
Residuals are evaluated in finite arithmetic using declared norms, scaling conventions, and nonnegative tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A numerical status-reliability signature prevents unconditional acceptance of a claimed optimal status but does not, by itself, establish the cause of the failure.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets, p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets, p. 23

children.title: Unknown Status Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Meaning and reporting implications of indeterminate, ambiguous, unsupported, or unclassified termination statuses.

assumptions_latex: The solver terminates without issuing a status supported by the declared acceptance tests.
All available candidate vectors and diagnostic measurements are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unknown status means that no supported conclusion was obtained; it is not equivalent to any mathematical LP status.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unknown is an epistemic outcome of the run, not a property of the LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) contain the statuses admitted by the benchmark's certificate rules. Interpret \(\widehat\sigma=\mathrm{unknown}\) as the assertion that the run produced no status in \(\mathcal C\) whose acceptance predicate was satisfied. Consequently, unknown does not imply infeasibility, unboundedness, absence of an optimum, or numerical failure; it records insufficient reliable evidence to select among those possibilities. Candidate iterates, bounds, residuals, termination reasons, and numerical warnings may be reported separately, but none changes the status without satisfying its corresponding certificate predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown means the run established no accepted status. It must not be interpreted as infeasible, unbounded, optimal, or necessarily numerically failed.
knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Status Interpretation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly treats unknown as epistemic rather than as an LP status, but solver-status and certificate semantics require an authoritative source.

children.title: Status Reliability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which returned termination labels lack sufficient evidence for dependable benchmark classification.

assumptions_latex: Each reported status \(q\) has a declared acceptance predicate \(C_q(d)\) on diagnostic data \(d\).
Diagnostic quantities use declared tolerances, norms, and scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A status is reliable only inside the region where its predicate is satisfied and no invalidating numerical condition is present.

notation.meaning: Diagnostic data returned by a run

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary is defined by certificate predicates, not solver status labels alone.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets, p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a solver label \(q\), define its reliability region by \(\mathcal R_q=\{d:C_q(d)=\mathrm{true}\text{ and }N(d)=\mathrm{false}\}\). A returned label \(q\) is accepted as reliable exactly when \(d\in\mathcal R_q\). If \(C_q(d)\) fails, cannot be evaluated, or conflicts with another accepted certificate, the run lies outside the reliability boundary and must be classified as uncertain or inconsistent. Tolerances and scaling used by \(C_q\) are part of the boundary and must remain fixed when results are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A status is reliable only when its declared certificate passes, no numerical warning invalidates it, and no conflicting certificate is accepted.
knowledge_statements.title: Status Reliability Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets, p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but the cited optimality-conditions page does not demonstrably support the generic status predicates, numerical invalidation rule, or conflict-handling policy.

children.title: Numerical Failure Evidence Capture
children.top_down_role: Solver logs, residual summaries, warnings, environment records, plus intermediate status information retained for diagnosis.

assumptions_latex: The solver exposes termination, residual, iteration, and linear-algebra diagnostics.
The benchmark protocol records configuration and platform metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting evidence record permits later evaluation of numerical signatures and status reliability without reconstructing missing run state.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capture occurs before cleanup can discard the state associated with numerical termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On numerical warning or uncertain termination, initialize \(E_{\rm num}\) with the instance identifier, solver version, parameters, platform, and random seed. Append the raw status, termination reason, elapsed time, iteration count, last candidate \((x,y,s)\), residual summary \(R\), objective and bound values, scaling data, factorization or arithmetic error codes, and the last finite diagnostic history. Mark unavailable fields explicitly. Recompute only declared derived checks from captured raw values, store their tolerances and norms, and output the immutable record \(E_{\rm num}\) together with, but distinct from, the benchmark classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On numerical or uncertain termination, capture raw status, configuration, candidate vectors, residuals, bounds, scaling, error codes, and diagnostic history before cleanup.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Failure Evidence Capture

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The procedural content appropriately uses the algorithm kind, but the proposed capture schema and recomputation policy lack an inspectable diagnostics or reproducibility source.

children.title: Cross-Solver Disagreement
children.top_down_role: Conflicting statuses, objective values, certificates, or accuracy assessments produced by different solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Solver Disagreement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational disagreement predicate for two solvers applied to one canonical LP instance under declared tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For solver reports \(R_i=(s_i,v_i,ho_i,q_i)\), where \(s_i\) is the termination status, \(v_i\) is the reported objective when available, \(ho_i\) is an independently recomputed maximum normalized residual, and \(q_i\) is the independently validated certificate class, define \[\Delta_v(R_1,R_2)= rac{|v_1-v_2|}{1+\max\{|v_1|,|v_2|\}}.\] At tolerances \(	au_v,	au_r\geq0\), cross-solver disagreement occurs when the solvers receive the same canonical LP data but \(s_1
eq s_2\), or both claim optimality and \(\Delta_v(R_1,R_2)>	au_v\), or \(\mathbf 1\{ho_1\leq	au_r\}
eq\mathbf 1\{ho_2\leq	au_r\}\), or \(q_1
eq q_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two solver results disagree when matched LP runs yield incompatible statuses, materially different optimal objectives, different residual acceptance outcomes, or different independently validated certificate classes.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) concern identical canonical LP data.
\(\tau_v\) and \(\tau_r\) are fixed before comparing the reports.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(R_1,R_2)=1\) exactly when at least one stated status, objective, residual, or certificate inconsistency occurs.

notation.meaning: Normalized diagnostic report from solver i.
Maximum independently recomputed normalized feasibility or optimality residual.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the cited implementation page does not establish this bespoke four-part disagreement predicate. Status normalization and certificate classes are unspecified, and Δ_v is written without restricting its domain to reports having objective values. An inspectable source or explicit local-convention rationale is required.

children.title: Version-Induced Drift
children.top_down_role: Behavioral or performance changes attributable to solver releases, dependency updates, or build revisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Version-Induced Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolates result drift caused by changing only the solver build or version.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_{v}(M,C,E)\) denote the normalized report produced by solver version \(v\) on canonical model \(M\), configuration \(C\), and execution environment \(E\). Version-induced drift at disagreement tolerances \(\tau\) occurs for versions \(v_a\neq v_b\) when \[D_{\tau}\bigl(F_{v_a}(M,C,E),F_{v_b}(M,C,E)\bigr)=1,\] while \(M\), \(C\), \(E\), input serialization, deterministic seed, and resource limits are held fixed. If any of these controls changes, the observation is confounded and does not by itself establish version-induced drift. The definition detects reproducible behavioral drift; it does not identify the internal software change causing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Version-induced drift is reproducible diagnostic disagreement after changing only the solver version; changes in model, configuration, environment, seed, or limits make the attribution inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: \(v_a\neq v_b\).
\(M\), \(C\), and \(E\) are reproducibly fixed.
\(D_{\tau}\) is a prespecified disagreement predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\tau}(F_{v_a}(M,C,E),F_{v_b}(M,C,E))=1\) constitutes version-induced drift only under the stated controls.

notation.meaning: Report-producing execution of solver version v.
Canonical model, normalized configuration, and controlled environment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the cited source does not support the stated controlled-experiment definition. Serialization, seed, and resource limits are required to remain fixed yet are not explicit arguments of F_v, leaving their encoding in C or E ambiguous. A source or declared local operational convention must specify the controls and attribution boundary.

children.title: Configuration-Matched Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparisons aligned by model data, tolerances, resource limits, execution environment, plus relevant solver settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Matched Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparability condition that controls solver inputs, numerical policies, stopping rules, and execution resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent run \(i\) by \(U_i=(M_i,P_i,T_i,A_i,S_i,L_i,E_i)\): canonical model, preprocessing and scaling policy, numerical tolerances, algorithm selection, randomness controls, stopping and resource limits, and numerical environment. Two runs are configuration-matched when \[M_1=M_2,\quad P_1=P_2,\quad T_1=T_2,\quad A_1=A_2,\quad S_1=S_2,\quad L_1=L_2,\quad E_1=E_2,\] after translating solver-specific options into declared semantic categories. Unsupported or undocumented options are recorded as unmatched rather than silently treated as equal. Under this condition, a remaining report disagreement is not explained by any recorded configuration field, although unrecorded implementation differences may remain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runs are configuration-matched only when canonical data and all declared preprocessing, tolerance, algorithm, randomness, stopping, resource, and environment controls agree semantically.
assumptions_latex: \(M_i\) is a canonical, byte-reproducible representation of the LP.
Solver-specific options admit an explicit semantic normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_1\sim U_2\) if and only if every displayed normalized comparison field is equal.

notation.meaning: Normalized execution specification for run i.
Canonical LP model supplied to run i.

source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate, but the cited general implementation sections do not substantiate this exact comparability relation. Equality after translating solver-specific algorithms and options requires a defined normalization map and field domains; otherwise the displayed equalities are not independently checkable.

children.title: Disagreement Triage Evidence
children.top_down_role: Artifacts used to localize conflicts across solvers, versions, configurations, or numerical environments.

knowledge_statements.title: Disagreement Triage Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum reproducible evidence bundle for independently classifying an LP solver disagreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a canonical LP \(M\) and compared runs \(U_1,U_2\), a disagreement-triage certificate is a bundle \(B=(M,U_1,U_2,R_1,R_2,V_1,V_2)\), where each \(R_i\) contains the raw status, solution, objective, bounds, log, and claimed certificate, and \(V_i\) contains independently recomputed primal residual, dual residual, bound violation, objective, and primal-dual gap. The bundle is verifiable when it fixes data serialization, solver version, normalized configuration, tolerances, and arithmetic used for validation. It certifies certificate-level disagreement when exactly one \(V_i\) satisfies the declared acceptance inequalities; if both or neither satisfy them, causal triage remains unresolved without additional evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triage certificate records reproducible inputs, configurations, raw reports, logs, and independently recomputed residuals, objectives, violations, and gaps; asymmetric validation identifies certificate-level disagreement.
assumptions_latex: \(U_1\sim U_2\) under the declared matching relation.
Validation tolerances are fixed independently of the observed reports.
Each validation quantity is recomputed from canonical data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf 1\{V_1\text{ is accepted}\}\neq\mathbf 1\{V_2\text{ is accepted}\}\) certifies certificate-level disagreement, but not its internal software cause.

notation.meaning: Raw report and artifacts from run i.
Independent numerical validation record for run i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind is plausible for this evidence leaf, but the cited page does not support the proposed minimum bundle or certification rule. The tuple B omits explicit acceptance inequalities, tolerances, and validation arithmetic that the prose requires. Moreover, asymmetric numerical acceptance certifies validation-outcome disagreement, not necessarily disagreement between certificate classes. Authoritative support and a precise certificate criterion are required.
